articles.title: SC Ports secures nearly 160,000 containers of new business
articles.summary: South Carolina Ports (SC Ports) has secured nearly 160,000 containers of new business as part of its strategy to restore growth and strengthen its competitive position. articles.body: South Carolina Ports (SC Ports) has secured nearly 160,000 containers of new business as part of its strategy to restore growth and strengthen its competitive position. The port authority is also expanding its focus on retail, manufacturing and refrigerated cargo. SC Ports President and CEO Micah Mallace outlined the progress during his second State of the Port address on 27 October. He highlighted a 20% reduction in expenses, new commercial commitments and ongoing infrastructure improvements. The additional business covers retail, consumer goods, manufacturing and export commodities. According to SC Ports, the new volumes will gradually enter its operations through 2027. The port authority attributed these gains to stronger sales efforts, more competitive rates and improved customer service. Its cost-cutting programme has also helped bring pricing back in line with competing ports. “We are a highly productive port, with ample capacity, a customer-focused mindset and the market fundamentals to thrive,” said Micah Mallace, President and CEO of SC Ports. “We are perfectly positioned to achieve above-market growth, and we are now starting to see that momentum generate.” Recent commercial developments include a new transloading facility near the port for a global retailer. National retail brands and major importers have also committed additional cargo to Charleston, selecting the port as a gateway for shipments into the southeastern United States. SC Ports is also strengthening its position in advanced manufacturing. Inland Port Greer has attracted more business from companies seeking access to rail connections. In October, the facility received its first container associated with Isuzu’s new commercial truck plant in Greenville County. Industrial property activity around Charleston has also improved. According to Cushman & Wakefield, approximately 5 million square feet of industrial space had been leased in the market so far in 2026. SC Ports expects several major leases to support additional cargo volumes. Terminal expansion and rail connectivity SC Ports is advancing several infrastructure projects to support future growth and improve connections with inland markets. Work has started on expanding the rail-served North Charleston Terminal. The project is expected to create additional cargo opportunities in the short term while increasing container-handling capacity over time. Meanwhile, the port authority continues working toward the resumption of operations at Leatherman Terminal. It is also progressing plans to bring the Navy Base Intermodal Facility into service. Mallace emphasized the importance of rail connectivity for customers moving goods between inland manufacturing and distribution centers and the Port of Charleston. Alongside these investments, SC Ports plans to attract more retail distribution centers and refrigerated cargo operations. The strategy aims to complement its established manufacturing business and create a more diversified cargo base. According to Mallace, a broader mix of cargo will improve the port’s resilience and support growth across South Carolina. However, the port authority acknowledged that overall cargo volumes remain below previous levels. Mallace noted that port development follows long investment cycles, meaning the benefits of recently secured business will emerge gradually. “The business being awarded today will pay dividends for years to come,” Mallace said. “Momentum begets momentum, and we have started to generate ours.”

The port authority is also expanding its focus on retail, manufacturing and refrigerated cargo.

articles.title: Patrick Terminals launches digital app for truck drivers
articles.summary: Patrick Terminals has launched Patrick Connect, a new mobile application designed to provide truck drivers with real-time information and operational guidance during visits to its container terminals in Australia. The app provides step-by-step instructions throughout the terminal visit, including lane assignments and...
articles.body: Patrick Terminals has launched Patrick Connect, a new mobile application designed to provide truck drivers with real-time information and operational guidance during visits to its container terminals in Australia. The app provides step-by-step instructions throughout the terminal visit, including lane assignments and access to compliance information such as weigh-in-motion (WIM) results. It also allows terminal operations teams to send safety notifications and operational updates directly to drivers. According to Patrick Terminals, the platform aims to improve communication between drivers and terminal staff while reducing the need for in-person interactions. Drivers can access relevant information digitally as they move through different stages of the terminal process. Patrick Connect has completed a trial at Patrick Terminals’ Sydney AutoStrad facility and is now ready for rollout to transport operators. The company plans to onboard additional users over the coming months. “Transport operators are key to our market-leading landside operations. Patrick Connect puts the information drivers need directly in their hands, from the moment they arrive at the gate to the moment they leave,” said Bruce Guy, Terminal Manager at Patrick Terminals – Sydney AutoStrad. “It’s a practical tool that makes every terminal visit clearer, safer and more efficient,” he added. The launch forms part of Patrick Terminals’ broader investment in landside technology and digital infrastructure. Previous improvements across its terminals include automated gates, upgraded truck grids, truck management systems and digital booking platforms. By bringing operational instructions, compliance information and safety communications into a single application, Patrick Terminals aims to simplify information access for transport operators and support more efficient coordination between terminal operations and road transport. The company said it will continue investing in infrastructure and digital systems to strengthen the productivity and resilience of Australia’s supply chains.

articles.title: Noatum Logistics doubles GCC truck fleet to over 850 vehicles
articles.summary: Noatum Logistics, the logistics arm of AD Ports Group, has doubled its trucking fleet to more than 850 vehicles as part of its expansion across the Middle East and Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) markets. The new trucks were delivered in batches over the past six months and have already been integrated into the...
articles.body: Noatum Logistics, the logistics arm of AD Ports Group, has doubled its trucking fleet to more than 850 vehicles as part of its expansion across the Middle East and Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) markets. The new trucks were delivered in batches over the past six months and have already been integrated into the company’s regional operations. All newly acquired vehicles meet Euro 5 emissions standards, supporting the expansion of its transport capacity across the region. The investment strengthens Noatum Logistics’ predominantly owned and operated fleet. It also allows the company to offer cross-border road transport as an in-house service, supporting its freight forwarding, contract logistics and project logistics activities. According to the company, the larger fleet will provide greater operational flexibility and improve its ability to respond to changing customer requirements across regional supply chains. “This investment is about much more than adding trucks. It is about building the capabilities that enable us to stay closer to our customers, deliver greater certainty and efficiency across their supply chains, and respond quickly to changing market conditions,” said Thorsten Pook, Managing Director of Noatum Logistics for the Middle East, Indian Subcontinent and CIS. Strengthening multimodal connections across the GCC Alongside its expanded road transport capacity, Noatum Logistics is combining its trucking operations with a dedicated rail shuttle service connecting Khalifa Port and Fujairah Terminals in the UAE. The company said the two transport modes complement each other in terms of capacity, cargo volumes and transit requirements. This combination allows customers to access alternative overland routes and maintain cargo movements during regional disruptions. The multimodal network also supports bonded transport corridors linking the UAE’s industrial centres with regional seaports and airports. According to Noatum Logistics, these connections provide additional options for customers seeking to maintain supply chain continuity. The fleet expansion is accompanied by investments in digital monitoring systems. Every vehicle is equipped with GPS tracking and connected to a centralised control tower, allowing the company to monitor vehicle movements, shipment progress and asset utilisation in real time. These capabilities are intended to improve shipment visibility and give customers greater oversight of their regional transport operations. The latest expansion follows other investments in Noatum Logistics’ road transport capabilities. In August, Container News reported on the delivery of electric heavy trucks to Noatum Logistics by SANY , highlighting the company’s wider efforts to develop its transport fleet. Backed by AD Ports Group, Noatum Logistics continues to expand its regional logistics network through investments in road, rail and digital infrastructure. The company aims to strengthen its position in cross-border transport while supporting more flexible supply chain connections across the GCC.

The new trucks were delivered in batches over the past six months and have already been integrated into the company’s regional operations.
All newly acquired vehicles meet Euro 5 emissions standards, supporting the expansion of its transport capacity across the region.

articles.summary: Four Romanian public officials and two other defendants have been indicted over the alleged fraudulent procurement of two tugboats that were supposed to improve navigation on the Lower Danube River...

Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Wojciech Wrzesien/Shutterstock Four Romanian public officials and two other defendants have been indicted over the alleged fraudulent procurement of two tugboats that were supposed to improve navigation on the Lower Danube River but were delivered with drafts too deep for their intended operations. The European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) announced Monday that it had filed charges against four officials from Romania’s Lower Danube River Administration (AFDJ Gala?i), an individual, and a company in connection with the €7 million project, which was financed through the European Union’s 2014–2020 Large Infrastructure Operational Programme. The two multipurpose, ice-class tugboats were intended to support navigation along the Lower Danube, including during periods of low water, and assist vessels in distress. However, prosecutors allege that the tender process was deliberately structured to favor a single supplier. According to the EPPO, the procurement specifications included technical requirements designed for seagoing vessels, even though the tugboats were intended for inland waterways. The requirements effectively restricted competition and favored one company. The vessels were delivered in 2021, but prosecutors say they failed to meet a critical contractual requirement. Both tugboats had an actual draft of 2.6 meters, exceeding the maximum allowable draft of two meters specified in the contract. Despite the discrepancy, the four public officials allegedly approved the vessels and signed final acceptance documents falsely certifying that the tugboats met the required technical specifications. The additional 60 centimeters of draft significantly limits where and when the vessels can operate safely on the Danube, particularly during periods of low water—the very conditions they were intended to help address. An individual and a company are also accused of assisting in the alleged scheme. Prosecutors estimate that the procurement caused approximately €7 million in losses to the EU budget, effectively putting the entire EU-funded investment at issue. The indictment has been filed with a court in Ia?i, Romania. If convicted, the defendants face prison sentences ranging from three to ten and a half years. The EPPO, which investigates and prosecutes crimes affecting the European Union’s financial interests, emphasized that all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty. The case highlights the consequences of procurement failures in publicly funded maritime infrastructure projects, particularly when vessels delivered under government contracts cannot fully perform the operations for which they were purchased. articles.title: Los Angeles, Long Beach Ports Identify LNG and Methanol as Leading Alternative Marine Fuels
articles.summary: The ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach have identified liquefied natural gas (LNG) and methanol as the most viable alternative marine fuels for the near and medium term, with...

Photo courtesy Port of Los Angeles The ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach have identified liquefied natural gas (LNG) and methanol as the most viable alternative marine fuels for the near and medium term, with a new study outlining potential demand and the infrastructure needed to support cleaner shipping at the nation’s busiest port complex. The joint Clean Marine Fuel Feasibility Assessment , conducted as part of the ports’ Green Shipping Corridor initiatives, examined which alternative fuels shipping companies are most likely to adopt, how demand could develop through 2030, and what investments would be needed to support bunkering operations. The study estimates that annual LNG demand at the San Pedro Bay ports could reach between 65,000 and 115,000 metric tons by 2030, while methanol demand could range from 64,000 to 250,000 metric tons, depending on market conditions and the deployment of alternative-fuel vessels. The findings come as shipping companies increasingly invest in dual-fuel vessels capable of running on alternatives to conventional marine fuels, although the industry has yet to settle on a single long-term solution. Approximately 4,000 vessels call at the two Southern California ports annually. Emissions from oceangoing vessels represent the largest source of emissions within the port complex, making cleaner marine fuels a central part of the ports’ efforts to meet their Clean Air Action Plan goals. “Strategic investments guided by this study will enable a growing market for these green marine fuels, helping ships serving the trans-Pacific transition to a cleaner future,” said Port of Long Beach CEO Dr. Noel Hacegaba. Rather than recommending large-scale infrastructure investments immediately, the assessment calls for a phased approach that takes advantage of existing facilities while supporting early adoption. For methanol, the study found that much of the necessary storage and distribution infrastructure is already available or could be adapted for marine fueling, potentially reducing upfront costs. The ports are encouraged to pursue pilot bunkering projects, provide incentives for early methanol adoption, and work with regulators to establish clear safety and permitting requirements. For LNG, the study recommends relying primarily on existing ship-to-ship bunkering methods rather than constructing major new storage facilities within the ports. The report also acknowledges that the environmental benefits of alternative marine fuels depend heavily on how they are produced and sourced. LNG and methanol can offer emissions reductions, but their overall climate impacts vary significantly depending on feedstocks, production methods and fuel supply chains. Fuel prices, regulatory requirements and commitments from shipping lines will ultimately determine how quickly demand develops. “Reducing emissions from ships is one of the most important challenges facing our industry,” said Port of Los Angeles Executive Director Gene Seroka. “This study gives us a clearer picture of where the market is headed and how we can work with our partners to make cleaner marine fuels more accessible.” The assessment builds on ongoing efforts to establish green shipping corridors connecting major international trading hubs. In April, the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach renewed their Green and Digital Shipping Corridor agreement with Singapore, with the partners committing to advance alternative-fuel bunkering, demonstration projects and digital connectivity. Singapore has already conducted methanol bunkering trials and awarded licenses to methanol fuel suppliers, while the Southern California ports have been working toward their own demonstration capabilities. The next step will be a joint request for proposals, expected by the end of 2026, seeking projects to demonstrate alternative-fuel bunkering capabilities in San Pedro Bay. The ports said the study will also guide future planning and coordination with shipping companies, fuel suppliers, terminal operators and government agencies as the industry works toward lower-emission operations. For now, the findings suggest that LNG and methanol are likely to play leading roles in the region’s marine fuel transition, with infrastructure development proceeding alongside actual demand rather than ahead of it. articles.title: Patrick Terminals to launch OptiBook at Sydney AutoStrad
articles.summary: Patrick Terminals and OneStop will launch the OptiBook container management platform at the Sydney AutoStrad Terminal on 28 November 2026, introducing a new booking system designed to improve container visibility and landside operations. The platform integrates with the OneStop Vehicle Booking System and provides...
articles.body: Patrick Terminals and OneStop will launch the OptiBook container management platform at the Sydney AutoStrad Terminal on 28 November 2026, introducing a new booking system designed to improve container visibility and landside operations. The platform integrates with the OneStop Vehicle Booking System and provides transport operators with information on container status, availability and timeslot bookings. It also connects with the OneStop Deliver App, allowing users to access booking and manifest information in real time. According to the companies, OptiBook aims to simplify the booking process while improving transparency across the landside supply chain. The system was developed in consultation with transport operators, incorporating industry feedback into its functionality. To prepare operators for the transition, Patrick Terminals and OneStop held an OptiBook Carrier Engagement Forum on 28 October. The session introduced the platform’s main features and outlined the changes ahead of its launch. OneStop has also scheduled two online training sessions for transport operators on 17 and 26 November. The company will provide registration details, supporting documentation and instructions for using the OneStop Deliver App ahead of implementation. “With all major terminals on one booking system, we can give transport operators and their systems a single, connected way to book, and that’s the foundation for much of what we’re building next,” said Chris Harnett, Chief Commercial Officer of OneStop. Bruce Guy, Terminal Manager at Patrick Terminals – Sydney AutoStrad, said the transition would provide a booking system capable of supporting the terminal’s operations over the longer term. “OptiBook gives Sydney AutoStrad a fully supported booking system for the long term, while maintaining the efficiencies our customers rely on today,” said Guy. The Sydney rollout follows the planned introduction of OptiBook at Patrick Terminals Brisbane and forms part of the company’s broader adoption of digital container management solutions. Container News previously reported on Patrick Terminals’ plans to introduce the container management platform as part of its efforts to improve landside operations. The upcoming launch will further consolidate container booking processes across major terminals using the OneStop platform.

articles.title: U.S. Senator Demands Russian Diesel Tanker Turn Around as Legal Fight Escalates
articles.summary: U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) is demanding that a tanker reportedly carrying Russian diesel to the United States reverse course, warning its owner that delivering the cargo would violate federal...

Join the leading maritime news network Stock Photo: Garry2014 / Shutterstock U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) is demanding that a tanker reportedly carrying Russian diesel to the United States reverse course, warning its owner that delivering the cargo would violate federal law despite authorization from the Trump administration. In an October 27 letter , Blumenthal called on Greek shipowner Eastern Mediterranean Maritime Limited (EASTMED) to recall the Malta-flagged Agioi Fanendes , which reportedly loaded nearly 40,000 metric tons of diesel at Russia’s Baltic port of Primorsk on October 22. The tanker was signaling the Port of New York and New Jersey as its destination, with an expected arrival date of November 7, according to shipping data cited in the letter. The demand marks a further escalation in the growing dispute over President Donald Trump’s agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to resume Russian diesel exports to the United States and global markets. “Should you confirm that this vessel intends to offload Russian diesel fuel at the Port of New York and New Jersey – or any other destination in the United States – we demand that you recall the Agioi Fanendes and to refrain from future transactions in Russian diesel in accordance with U.S. law,” Blumenthal wrote to EASTMED Managing Director Athanasios J. Martinos. The senator warned that delivering the cargo could expose the shipowner to legal consequences under the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act, passed by Congress in 2022 following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The legislation prohibits imports of Russian-origin petroleum products, including diesel. However, the Trump administration has issued Treasury General License 135 authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel through April 7, 2027, creating a dispute over whether the administration has the legal authority to permit imports otherwise prohibited by statute. Blumenthal argues that it does not. “We recognize that the Treasury Department issued General License No. 135 which reports to authorize transactions for Russia’s diesel exports, but no such license can supersede clear, unambiguous law,” he wrote. “The President may have given a license to facilitate this transaction, but only Congress can make it legally valid.” The Treasury Department maintains that the arrangement is legal, while the White House has defended the agreement as a measure to ease fuel costs amid supply disruptions caused by the war with Iran. In a separate public statement, Blumenthal said he was sending a “sledgehammer message” to shipping companies transporting Russian diesel toward American ports. “Reverse course while there’s still time,” he warned, adding that the administration’s license would not absolve companies of legal or moral accountability. Beyond demanding that the tanker turn around, Blumenthal is seeking detailed information about the companies involved in the shipment. EASTMED has been asked to identify the cargo’s seller, purchaser, charterer, insurer or protection and indemnity (P&I) provider, terminal operator, and any entity responsible for distribution. The senator also wants to know whether the company received instructions from the Treasury Department or any other federal agency regarding the shipment. The deadline for a response is October 31. The inquiry extends congressional scrutiny beyond the companies directly purchasing or importing Russian fuel to the shipowners, insurers and other maritime service providers involved in transporting it. The latest warning follows an October 24 letter from a bipartisan group of lawmakers urging major U.S. banks and port authorities to avoid facilitating Russian diesel imports. That earlier letter, signed by six senators and one House member, called on financial institutions and port authorities in Texas and New York to preserve records related to Russian diesel transactions, including shipping documents, contracts and communications with government officials. The lawmakers warned that companies participating in the trade could face future congressional investigations. The dispute comes as the first shipments begin moving under Trump’s October 9 agreement with Putin, which was intended to increase diesel supplies and ease soaring fuel prices. Under the agreement, Russia committed to supplying an initial 300,000 metric tons of diesel, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons thereafter. Reuters reported on October 23 that the Agioi Fanendes had loaded approximately 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low-sulfur diesel at Primorsk, citing LSEG shipping data. The identities of the buyer and seller were not immediately known. For shipowners and other maritime companies, the congressional pressure adds another layer of uncertainty to a trade that the administration has moved to reopen. Although Treasury has authorized qualifying transactions, lawmakers are warning that participants could still face legal challenges over shipments they contend violate the 2022 import ban. Whether those warnings will affect the Agioi Fanendes ‘ planned voyage to New York remains unclear. articles.title: MARAD Approves $8.2 Billion Texas LNG Export Port in Record-Time Review
articles.summary: The Trump administration has approved an $8.2 billion offshore liquefied natural gas export project off the Texas coast, marking a major milestone for its effort to speed up deepwater port...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Evgenii Bakhchev/Shutterstock The Trump administration has approved an $8.2 billion offshore liquefied natural gas export project off the Texas coast, marking a major milestone for its effort to speed up deepwater port licensing by shifting oversight from the U.S. Coast Guard to the Maritime Administration. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced Wednesday that the Maritime Administration (MARAD) has approved the deepwater port license application for ST LNG, LLC, a proposed LNG export facility approximately 10.4 miles offshore Matagorda, Texas. The project is expected to begin construction in 2027 and enter service in 2029, adding up to 8.4 million metric tons of annual LNG export capacity. According to the Department of Transportation, the $8.2 billion development could support 2,000 construction jobs and as many as 855 permanent positions. But the approval is also significant for how quickly it was completed. MARAD finalized the project’s Final Environmental Impact Statement (FEIS) in just 410 days, roughly 3.7 years faster than the historical average and a 70% reduction in review time, according to DOT. The administration described it as the fastest deepwater port license review in more than two decades. The decision provides an early test of a regulatory overhaul that gCaptain reported on earlier this year , when the Trump administration announced that MARAD would assume the lead role in reviewing deepwater port applications from the Coast Guard. Under the new arrangement, MARAD leads the environmental review and licensing process, while the Coast Guard retains responsibility for maritime safety, security, vessel traffic, facility design and operational oversight. The change was intended to address longstanding delays in approving offshore energy infrastructure. As gCaptain previously reported, only 11 deepwater port applications had been approved since the federal licensing system was established in the 1970s, with just eight licenses issued. The administration has argued that lengthy reviews have become an obstacle to expanding U.S. energy exports. “By slashing red tape and modernizing our licensing processes, the Trump Administration is delivering a massive economic boom for the people of Texas,” Duffy said Wednesday. MARAD Administrator Stephen Carmel called the ST LNG decision the agency’s third deepwater port approval under the Trump administration. “Approving the ST LNG deepwater port license—our third approval under the Trump Administration—proves we can accelerate the safe development of crucial energy infrastructure that will strengthen our supply chains and drive down energy prices,” Carmel said. Unlike conventional onshore LNG export terminals, ST LNG would process and load natural gas offshore, allowing LNG carriers to operate away from congested coastal port facilities. The project calls for four liquefaction systems, each capable of producing 2.1 million metric tons of LNG annually. At full buildout, the facility would include 20 offshore platforms, four floating LNG storage units, four vessel mooring systems and approximately 7.7 miles of pipeline. Natural gas would be supplied from the Tres Palacios Natural Gas Storage and Trading Hub and the Williams Markham Gas Processing Plant through existing pipeline infrastructure. The offshore location is intended to reduce vessel traffic in congested coastal waterways and limit potential collision risks associated with LNG shipping. According to DOT, the facility could expand U.S. LNG export capacity by 7% to 9%. The licensing decision follows a series of regulatory milestones over the past year. MARAD formally began processing the ST LNG application in 2025, published the draft environmental impact statement in April 2026 and issued the final environmental impact statement in July. A final public hearing was held in August before the agency reached its licensing decision. The review involved the Coast Guard, other federal agencies and the State of Texas. DOT credited the shortened timeline to eliminating duplicative administrative procedures, streamlining decision-making and improving coordination among agencies. The approval also advances the administration’s broader maritime and energy policies, including its executive orders on American energy production and restoring U.S. maritime dominance. While the administration is presenting the ST LNG decision as evidence that the new system can move projects through federal review more quickly, the larger test will be whether the changes translate into more offshore terminals reaching construction and commercial operations. The full Record of Decision and supporting documents are available through Regulations.gov under docket MARAD-2025-0096 . articles.title: Russia Turns to Arctic WW2 Route to Export Grain
articles.summary: Russia, the world's largest wheat exporter, has turned to an Arctic World War II shipping route to export grain for the first time as the conflict in Ukraine stalls Black Sea trade and officials warn of risks in the NATO-controlled Baltic Sea.

REUTERS/Stringer MOSCOW, Oct 28 (Reuters) – Russia, the world’s largest wheat exporter, has turned to an Arctic World War II shipping route to export grain for the first time as the conflict in Ukraine stalls Black Sea trade and officials warn of risks in the NATO-controlled Baltic Sea. Russia and Ukraine have been attacking each other’s ports and vessels since the new grain marketing season started in July, bringing the once booming Black Sea agriculture trade to a standstill. Russia, keen to keep its key grain customers in the Middle East and Asia, sought to reroute exports to Baltic Sea ports, subsidizing rail transport from fertile southern regions, but also eyed opportunities in the Arctic. Murmansk Commercial Seaport and Demetra Holding, one of the country’s largest trading firms, said on Wednesday that the first shipment of 3,400 metric tons of grain from “key agricultural regions” is being loaded onto a vessel. Murmansk, which is located almost 2,000 km (1,240 miles) north of Moscow near the border with Norway, can be approached through neutral waters. Allied convoys used the port during World War II to deliver goods to the Soviet Union. “At a time when traditional export routes are facing restrictions, Murmansk Commercial Seaport is swiftly opening up an alternative route to foreign markets for Russian farmers,” the port said. According to shipping data and a market source, around 28,000 metric tons of wheat are due to be loaded in Murmansk onto a vessel heading to Morocco’s Casablanca port. Russia has rerouted its trade mostly to the Baltic Sea ports, which handled 1.2 million tons in September, accounting for over 60% of all seaborne grain exports. Companies have been repurposing fertilizer and coal terminals to handle grain. Some Kremlin officials have warned of risks from potential hostile actions by European NATO member countries in the area. All countries with access to the Baltic Sea except Russia are NATO members. Russia’s relations with Europe have deteriorated in recent months as the Kremlin accused European countries of direct military involvement in the conflict in Ukraine. European governments have rejected Russian accusations that they are directly involved, saying their military and financial support for Ukraine is aimed at helping Kyiv defend itself. Turkey, an importer of grain from Russia, led the effort to introduce a ceasefire and resume shipments in the Black Sea, but Russia said it is no longer interested in a new Black Sea grain deal. Turkey and the United Nations helped mediate the Black Sea Grain Initiative, which was agreed in July 2022 to allow the safe export of Ukrainian grain via the Black Sea. Russia withdrew from the agreement in 2023, complaining that its own food and fertilizer exports faced obstacles. REUTERS/Stringer (Bloomberg) — The US military said vessels that have no need to move between ports in the Gulf of Oman and the Strait of Hormuz should stay away, as tensions ratchet up in the region. “Due to the current geopolitical situation, vessels which do not need to transit the area are advised to remain well clear to avoid unnecessary delays to their voyage,” the US Naval Forces Central Command said in an advisory on Wednesday issued via the Joint Maritime Information Center. “Vessels transiting this area are advised to plan additional transit time to allow for increased traffic density and military blockade enforcement operations,” the notice said. It remains unclear what prompted the advisory. The US military last publicly issued a similar notice in mid-July, when it began its blockade of Iranian shipping. Back then, it said that the blockade would not impede neutral passage through Hormuz, though ships should expect to be questioned on their intentions. Traffic through the chokepoint has recovered in recent months, with shuttle tankers making up a big part of the traffic carrying crude oil. These ships make multiple runs in and out of the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman, where other tankers unwilling to risk the Strait await to receive cargoes. Dozens of crude tankers willing to take the risk have helped lift oil flows from the Persian Gulf to near prewar levels, while the US blockade has pushed Iranian crude exports close to zero. At the same time, Iran has been ramping up its attacks on ships to a wartime high of almost 30 in October. The latest US advisory said that neutral vessels with neutral cargo or are in ballast sailing between these neutral ports may be subject to questioning, visit, and search to confirm their intentions regarding the blockade. The US Central Command and the US Naval Forces Central Command — the naval unit that is part of Centcom and oversees the naval blockade of Iran — did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.title: Scorpio Tankers Reports $181,000-a-Day LR2 Rates as Middle East War Upends Oil Trade
articles.summary: Scorpio Tankers is reporting a sharp surge in tanker earnings as the war in the Middle East disrupts global oil flows, with its LR2 product tankers securing bookings averaging $181,000...

Join the leading maritime news network Stock Image: MartinLueke / Shutterstock.com Scorpio Tankers is reporting a sharp surge in tanker earnings as the war in the Middle East disrupts global oil flows, with its LR2 product tankers securing bookings averaging $181,000 per day so far in the fourth quarter. The figure represents a roughly 150% increase from the $72,283 per day its LR2 fleet earned during the third quarter, highlighting the extraordinary freight market conditions facing tanker operators as the conflict reshapes trade routes and vessel availability. In its third-quarter earnings release Wednesday, Scorpio said the war has disrupted traditional shipping routes, lengthened voyages and left tankers geographically displaced, tightening vessel supply and pushing freight rates higher. The strength extends beyond the larger LR2 class. Scorpio’s medium-range (MR) product tankers have secured fourth-quarter bookings averaging $56,000 per day, up from $31,183 in the third quarter, while Handymax tankers are averaging $40,000 per day, compared with $24,253 previously. The fourth-quarter figures are preliminary, covering 44% of expected revenue days for LR2s, 47% for MRs and 37% for Handymax vessels. Actual earnings for the full quarter will depend on rates secured for the remaining days. The surge comes as the conflict involving Iran continues to disrupt maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waterways, forcing changes to established oil trading patterns and increasing demand for available tonnage. The disruption has also affected the balance between crude and product tanker markets. With larger vessels drawn into crude oil trades, fewer LR2s are available to transport refined products, adding further pressure to freight rates. For Scorpio, one of the world’s largest product tanker operators, the market strength is translating into substantial profits even as the company operates a smaller fleet. Scorpio reported third-quarter net income of $224.3 million, up approximately 165% from a year earlier, while adjusted net income reached $127.4 million. Reported earnings included $152.6 million in gains from vessel sales. The company’s average operating fleet declined from 99 vessels in the third quarter of 2025 to approximately 75 vessels during the latest quarter. Despite the reduction, average daily time-charter-equivalent earnings climbed from $26,231 to $37,508. For the first nine months of 2026, Scorpio reported net income of $828.1 million, including significant gains from asset sales. The company is also using its financial strength to expand its exposure to the crude tanker market. Scorpio has four very large crude carriers (VLCCs) on order, including two vessels contracted in September at China’s Hengli Shipbuilding for $135 million each. It also holds a minority interest in a joint venture developing eight additional VLCC newbuildings scheduled for delivery between 2029 and 2030. Separately, Scorpio invested $38.4 million in Volare Shipping during its October initial public offering, acquiring a 3.4% stake in the crude tanker operator. The investments mark a notable expansion beyond Scorpio’s traditional focus on refined petroleum products, positioning the company for potential growth in the crude oil transportation market. Scorpio reported approximately $2.1 billion in unrestricted cash as of October 26 and announced an increase in its quarterly dividend to $0.75 per share from $0.45. While the company’s latest earnings reflect unusually strong market conditions, the fourth-quarter booking figures offer an indication of just how dramatically the Middle East conflict has changed tanker economics. Whether those rates can be sustained will depend heavily on how the conflict evolves and how quickly normal trading patterns can be restored. articles.title: T. Parker Host Invests $50 Million to Expand Former Avondale Shipyard
articles.summary: T. Parker Host (HOST) is investing $50 million to expand rail, warehouse and dock capacity at Avondale Global Gateway, the former Avondale Shipyard site on the Mississippi River near New...

Parker Host has announced a $50 million investment to expand the former shipyard's dock, rail and warehouse capacity. (Photo: T. Parker Host) T. Parker Host (HOST) is investing $50 million to expand rail, warehouse and dock capacity at Avondale Global Gateway, the former Avondale Shipyard site on the Mississippi River near New Orleans, as demand grows for industrial cargo handling and logistics infrastructure. The investment, announced Wednesday, will include a new 200,000-square-foot warehouse, expanded rail infrastructure and improvements to the facility’s deepwater docks. The project is expected to be completed by December 2027. The new warehouse will bring Avondale’s total indoor storage capacity to approximately 2 million square feet and will be the first new building constructed at the site since the 1970s. HOST also plans to activate Avondale’s fifth deepwater dock, increasing the facility’s capacity to handle up to six vessels simultaneously. The $50 million capital program includes $15 million for rail improvements, $15 million for the warehouse, $5 million for dock upgrades, $5 million for roads, $5 million for expanded site and laydown capacity, and another $5 million for equipment. “We’re building Avondale for what comes next,” said Adam Anderson, chairman and CEO of T. Parker Host. “When a company looks at Louisiana for its next major investment, we want the infrastructure to already be here. This $50 million investment gives our customers the ability to move faster and grow here for the long term.” The expansion is expected to create approximately 100 additional HOST jobs, bringing the company’s workforce at Avondale to more than 400 employees. With additional tenant developments anticipated, HOST expects approximately 1,000 people to be working across the industrial campus each day by 2028. The investment marks another step in the transformation of the former shipbuilding facility into a major multimodal logistics and industrial hub. Avondale has emerged as North America’s leading copper import terminal and recently secured a long-term agreement with a major energy equipment manufacturer. The facility also recently handled what HOST described as the first significant shipment of Venezuelan primary aluminum to the United States in more than eight years. HOST said growing demand for copper, power generation equipment and other industrial materials, including those used in data center construction and artificial intelligence infrastructure, is helping drive the need for additional capacity. The company expects the improvements to help attract hundreds of millions of dollars in additional private investment from industrial tenants. The expansion also includes $6.95 million in state and local support directed toward rail infrastructure. Louisiana Economic Development is providing a $2.6 million interest-free loan through its FastSites Program, while the Louisiana Legislature has approved $3.1 million in capital funding. Jefferson Parish has committed another $1.25 million. Work on the infrastructure improvements is already underway. Located in Jefferson Parish along the Mississippi River, Avondale Global Gateway handles more than 75 commodities and offers deepwater access, Class I rail connections, warehouse space and land for industrial development. HOST, which acquired the former shipyard property in 2018 , has been redeveloping the site as a logistics and manufacturing center, shifting its focus from ship construction to cargo handling, storage and industrial operations. The latest investment is intended to give customers additional capacity to establish long-term operations at the site, including processing and manufacturing activities, while strengthening Avondale’s role as an industrial gateway for the Gulf Coast. articles.title: First-of-its-kind marine robotics test and development center opens in Norway
articles.summary: Equinor has opened a new, dedicated facility in Norway for the testing, qualification and development of marine robotic technologies, such as...
articles.body: Technology & Innovation October 28, 2026 · 14 hours ago First-of-its-kind marine robotics test and development center opens in Norway NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Equinor Equinor has opened a new, dedicated facility in Norway for the testing, qualification and development of marine robotic technologies, such as subsea drones, robots and unmanned vessels. The Kårstø Marine Robotics Centre (KNARR) was opened on October 28 by Norway's Minister of Research and Higher Education, Eileen Fugelsnes, at the processing plant at Kårstø in Tysvær, on Norway's west coast. The center is an extension of several established test centers for the early phase of technology testing and is said to be Norway’s and one of the world’s first of its kind connected to a facility in operation, allowing the development of technology in an already operational environment. Three test areas have been set aside in water depths of 25, 140 and 250 meters, respectively. It will be available for use across the maritime industries and will, among other things, establish solutions for inspection, autonomous operations, environmental monitoring, securing and maintenance of offshore installations. According to Equinor, three kilometers of subsea cable and associated electronics have been laid to test sensor technology over time, which, together with existing power cables, export pipelines and subsea structures, provides an opportunity to test distributed acoustic sensing (DAS), among others. The company said that it had, together with Gassco, so far set aside NOK 16 million (around €1.5 million) to establish the center, revealing the possibility of expanding the facilities for new functionality in the future. (L-R): Hege Skryseth, Executive Vice President for Technology, Digitalization and Innovation at Equinor, and Eileen Fugelsnes, Minister of Research and Higher Education Photo: Torstein Lund Eik/ Equinor “The Norwegian continental shelf is important for a reliable and secure supply of oil and gas to Europe, and technology is crucial for maintaining oil and gas production and getting more value out of existing fields and infrastructure. At the KNARR centre, we can test and mature technology that makes offshore operations safer, more efficient and more data driven. This is done in close collaboration with suppliers, research communities and industry partners,” said Hege Skryseth , Executive Vice President for Technology, Digitalisation and Innovation at Equinor. “The strong environments we have in advanced robotics and digital technology in Norway are among the strategic advantages that will be able to strengthen our competitiveness in the decades to come. We have a long coast, and a rich maritime industrial history that we want to strengthen through good cooperation across industries such as aquaculture, oil and gas extraction, wind power, shipping and the defence industry.” Reach the Offshore Energy industry in one go! articles.title: Shell ups its production ante with first oil from US Gulf project’s third chapter
articles.summary: Shell has tied new wells into an existing floating oil facility, boosting deepwater output in the U.S. Gulf of Mexico (Gulf of America).
articles.body: Exploration & Production October 28, 2026 · 14 hours ago Shell ups its production ante with first oil from US Gulf project’s third chapter Shell has tied new wells into an existing floating oil facility, boosting deepwater output in the U.S. Gulf of Mexico (Gulf of America). MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Shell's Perdido oil production platform Source: Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement (BSEE) Shell Offshore, a subsidiary of the UK-headquartered energy giant Shell, has kicked off production at a new phase of its deepwater development project, leveraging its regional host infrastructure to add up to 6,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day (boe/d) at peak rates. Shell has brought online Phase 3 of the Silvertip project, which will deliver two wells to boost production at its operated Perdido spar in the Gulf of America. These wells in the Silvertip Frio reservoir, led by Shell (40%) in partnership with Chevron (60%), are expected to collectively produce up to 6,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day at peak rates. Colette Hirstius , Shell's Executive Vice President for GoA and Shell USA President, commented: "By adding new production through existing Perdido infrastructure, we can safely deliver more value and optimize the life of a world-class asset. "This is further proof of how we are making the most out of our assets in the GoA, helping to provide secure energy from one of the most competitive deep-water basins in the world." Shell is the operator of the Perdido Regional Host (PRH) and has a 35% working interest, with Chevron holding a 37.5% stake, 3C Perdido Holdings 26.5%, and BP 1% interest. Perdido is a production spar in the U.S. Gulf, located offshore within Alaminos Canyon, approximately 200 miles south of Galveston, Texas, in about 8,000 feet of water. The development concept for Phase 3 Silvertip entails two wells, tied into existing subsea infrastructure. The current estimated recoverable resource volumes of this project are 17 million boe. The estimate of resource volumes is currently classified as 2P under the Society of Petroleum Engineers' Resource Classification System. The Perdido offshore development comprises a spar platform that serves as a production hub for three deepwater fields: Silvertip, Tobago, and Great White. Shell recently wrapped up the sale of its 50% non-operated working interest in the Na Kika platform and associated fields in the Gulf of America as well as its 100% owned Coulomb tie-back to a subsidiary of Talos Energy and an affiliate of Ridgewood Energy. articles.title: Russia To Begin Year-Round Arctic Northern Sea Route Shipping in Early 2027
articles.summary: Russia expects to begin regular year-round eastbound shipping along the Northern Sea Route in early 2027, as additional nuclear icebreaker capacity, newer ice-class LNG carriers and pressure to redirect energy exports toward Asia bring the long-delayed ambition closer to reality.

(Source: Atomflot) Russia expects to begin regular year-round eastbound shipping along the Northern Sea Route in early 2027, as additional nuclear icebreaker capacity, newer ice-class LNG carriers and pressure to redirect energy exports toward Asia bring the long-delayed ambition closer to reality. Vladimir Panov, head of the Arctic Directorate at state nuclear corporation Rosatom, said that preparations for regular winter voyages were in their final stages. The planned start will coincide with one of Russia’s largest shippers beginning regular eastbound deliveries, he said, without identifying the company. Panov pointed to Novatek’s substantial LNG shipments along the route, as well as the start of oil exports from Rosneft’s Vostok Oil project . Six voyages carrying Vostok Oil cargoes have already been completed, he said. “[The Northern Sea Route] is one step away from regular shipments in the eastern direction, that is, one step away from year-round navigation,” Panov said, adding that Rosatom expects the transition to take place in early 2027. The timing would be significant for Novatek, Russia’s largest LNG producer. From Jan. 1, 2027, the European Union’s ban on Russian LNG imports under long-term contracts is scheduled to take effect , increasing the incentive to direct cargoes toward Asian buyers. Regular eastbound shipments would allow the company to move more LNG from its Arctic production facilities toward Asia without relying exclusively on seasonal navigation windows. Russia is also expanding its icebreaker fleet. The nuclear-powered Chukotka , the fourth serial Project 22220 icebreaker, is scheduled to enter service in early 2027, bringing the total number of operational nuclear icebreakers to nine , according to Panov. The additional capacity would complement a growing fleet of Arc7 ice-class LNG carriers, including newer-generation vessels designed for demanding winter conditions. Russia’s Zvezda shipyard has delivered two 2nd generation Arc7 gas carriers optimized for winter navigation. Winter navigation along the NSR is not new. In January 2021, Novatek sent several Arc7 LNG carriers through the eastern route, including Christophe de Margerie and Nikolay Yevgenov . While the former completed its passage without reported issues, Nikolay Yevgenov suffered damage to one of its three azimuth propulsion units near the Bering Strait, illustrating the mechanical risks associated with winter ice navigation. Further trials demonstrated that winter exports were technically possible. In December 2022 and January 2023, the Arc7 carrier Vladimir Voronin completed a round trip between the Yamal LNG terminal at Sabetta and China in 42 days, with nuclear icebreaker support during parts of the voyage. Arc7 carriers have also made late-spring voyages in May and early June. However, the most difficult late-winter period, particularly March and April, has remained a significant operational challenge. Russia previously aimed to establish year-round eastbound navigation in early 2024, with Rosatom and Novatek announcing the plan in 2023 . The proposed regular service did not materialize as scheduled, despite the successful trial voyages and changes to navigation rules that expanded the periods during which Arc7 vessels could sail independently. The conditions are now more favorable in several respects. Additional Project 22220 icebreakers are entering service, newer Arc7 vessels offer improved winter capabilities, and the loss of access to the EU market for Russian LNG under long-term contracts creates a stronger commercial incentive to develop winter routes. Yet the technical and logistical constraints remain. Panov acknowledged that increasing convoy speeds is a priority and that Russia must continue expanding emergency-response, communications and medical infrastructure along the route. articles.title: CMA CGM announces new Asia-Africa surcharges for November
articles.summary: CMA CGM has announced a series of Peak Season Surcharge (PSS) updates covering shipments from Asia to several African destinations, with charges reaching US$900 per TEU on selected routes from China to West Africa. The revised surcharges will take effect on 1 November 2026 and cover shipments to West, East and...
articles.body: CMA CGM has announced a series of Peak Season Surcharge (PSS) updates covering shipments from Asia to several African destinations, with charges reaching US$900 per TEU on selected routes from China to West Africa. The revised surcharges will take effect on 1 November 2026 and cover shipments to West, East and Southern Africa, alongside Madagascar, Mauritius, Seychelles and the Maldives. The French carrier has also announced a separate overweight surcharge for certain dry containers moving from China to East Africa. The highest announced PSS applies to shipments from China and its Special Administrative Regions (SARs) to the southern range of West Africa, covering Angola, Congo, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Namibia, Gabon and Cameroon. For dry and reefer cargo moving to these destinations under short-term contracts, CMA CGM will apply a surcharge of US$900 per TEU from 1 November, based on the loading date. Shipments from China and its SARs to the central West African range, including Nigeria, Côte d’Ivoire, Benin, Equatorial Guinea and Togo, will be subject to a PSS of US$700 per TEU. Ghana is excluded from this adjustment, with its existing surcharge remaining unchanged. For cargo destined for Senegal, the carrier has announced a PSS of US$400 per TEU, while charges for other destinations in the northern West African range remain unchanged. Separately, CMA CGM will apply a US$300 per TEU PSS on dry cargo shipments from Southeast Asia to West Africa under short-term contracts, also effective from 1 November. Additional surcharges across African trades The carrier has announced a US$300 per TEU PSS for all cargo moving from China to Madagascar, Mozambique, Mauritius and South Africa. The charge will apply from 1 November on short-term contracts. A further US$300 per TEU surcharge will apply to shipments from China to Mombasa in Kenya, Dar es Salaam and Zanzibar in Tanzania, and Port Victoria in Seychelles. CMA CGM has also announced a US$250 per TEU PSS for shipments from China, Southeast Asia and Northeast Asia to Malé in the Maldives, effective from the same date. In addition to the peak season adjustments, the company will introduce an Overweight Surcharge (OWS) of US$300 per container for 20-foot dry containers moving from China to East Africa with a gross weight exceeding 18 tonnes. The overweight charge will apply from 1 November 2026 until further notice and is separate from the carrier’s peak season surcharges. For shipments originating in China, CMA CGM noted that the relevant PSS adjustments will be subject to filing with the Shanghai Shipping Exchange and/or incorporated into ocean freight rates. The carrier also indicated that the announced surcharges are separate from applicable bunker-related charges, terminal handling charges, safety and security surcharges, and other local or contingency charges. The latest adjustments follow earlier CMA CGM surcharge announcements affecting Asia-Africa trades, reflecting further changes to the carrier’s pricing structure across several regional markets ahead of November.

articles.title: Germany’s SEFE firms up two-decade-long offtake deal with Canadian LNG project
articles.summary: A binding 20-year agreement has enabled Germany’s SEFE to secure 1 mtpa of Canadian LNG starting in the early 2030s.
articles.body: Business & Finance October 28, 2026 · 15 hours ago Germany’s SEFE firms up two-decade-long offtake deal with Canadian LNG project A binding 20-year agreement has enabled Germany’s SEFE to secure 1 mtpa of Canadian LNG starting in the early 2030s. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 3 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Ksi Lisims LNG concept Source: Rockies LNG In a move that deepens transatlantic energy ties and strengthens European security of supply amid a shifting global energy landscape, Germany’s Securing Energy for Europe (SEFE) has struck its first Canadian multi-year liquefied natural gas (LNG) deal to enable supplies from an LNG project, being developed on Canada’s northwest coast to export lower-carbon LNG to markets in Asia. The Nisga’a Nation-backed Ksi Lisims LNG project is moving closer to its construction phase after securing a binding sale and purchase agreement (SPA) to supply German state-backed energy firm SEFE with one million tonnes per annum (mtpa) of LNG on a free-on-board (FOB) basis, with the European firm signing on for two decades of low-carbon exports starting in the early 2030s. Frédéric Barnaud , SEFE’s CCO, underlined: “This agreement is an important step in further diversifying SEFE’s global LNG portfolio and securing reliable long-term energy supplies for our customers. Together with Ksi Lisims, we will help strengthen energy security while advancing the transition to a more sustainable energy system.” This is SEFE’s first agreement with a Canadian LNG supplier. The SPA follows a heads of agreement (HOA) inked in May 2026. Ksi Lisims LNG now has binding contracts for 7 mtpa of its 12 mtpa capacity and preliminary agreements for an additional 2 mtpa. Davis Thames , Founder, President, and CEO of Western LNG, commented: “We look forward to working with SEFE to provide its customers with reliable, low-carbon LNG. “Secure and diversified energy supply is fundamental to global economic prosperity, and our project is uniquely positioned to meet these priorities. The momentum behind Ksi Lisims LNG is stronger today than at any point in its development and we are excited about the months to come.” The Ksi Lisims LNG project was proposed by the Nisga’a Nation, Rockies LNG, and Western LNG. With capital costs of approximately $7.4 billion (around CAD 10 billion), the research done by the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) suggests that the cost could surge to $19.2 billion (about CAD 26 billion) for the project. This will depend on final design, infrastructure scope, and market conditions due to the evolving financial landscape surrounding major energy infrastructure projects. The Ksi Lisims LNG project remains on track to reach full commercialization by the end of the year. Eva Clayton , President of Nisga’a Lisims Government, said: “Each new agreement brings Ksi Lisims LNG closer to construction, and closer to the jobs, training and long-term revenue our people have worked toward for generations. “As a co-developer, our Nation is proving that Canada’s resources can reach world markets in a way that respects our lands and our rights. SEFE’s commitment shows the world is ready for that kind of partnership.” The 12-mtpa natural gas liquefaction and marine terminal project is envisioned to receive 1.7–2 billion cubic feet of natural gas per day and export it overseas once commercial operations start in late 2028 or 2029. The project obtained a 40-year export license from the Canada Energy Regulator (CER) two years before the first LNG offtake agreement was inked with Shell. Another German firm, Uniper, penned a 20-year SPA with Ksi Lisims LNG for the delivery of 2 mtpa of LNG a few months ago. With SEFE committing to purchase Canadian LNG for the next 20 years, we are seeing our ambition to diversify trade, strengthen transatlantic energy security, and make Canada a global energy superpower translate into real commercial results. “Led by the Nisga’a Nation, Ksi Lisims LNG demonstrates how Indigenous partnerships, Canadian energy expertise, and federal initiatives like the Major Projects Office can come together to build major projects, create good-paying jobs, and open new markets for Canadian resources.” Reach the Offshore Energy industry in one go! articles.body: Americas Offshore Noble offloads idle drillship for $38m Bojan Lepic October 28, 2026 0 1,122 1 minute read Noble Corporation Noble Corporation US offshore drilling contractor Noble Corporation has agreed to sell its 2013-built, sixth-generation drillship, Noble Globetrotter II, for $38m as it continues to dispose of underutilised drilling assets. The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026. Noble has not disclosed the buyer’s identity or the rig’s intended future use. However, chief executive Robert Eifler confirmed during the company’s third-quarter earnings call that the drillship would leave the offshore drilling fleet following the sale. The Noble Globetrotter II , designed to operate in water depths of up to 10,000 ft, has been idle since April 2024 after completing work for Shell in the US Gulf of Mexico. Noble first announced plans to dispose of the unit in August 2025, citing its prolonged inactivity and lack of competitiveness compared with other ultra-deepwater rigs in its marketed fleet. The sale follows the disposal of the Noble Resolve jackup, completed earlier this month, when the company received the remaining $45m in proceeds. Noble has also been pursuing a broader fleet rationalisation programme involving the sale of six jackups, including five units to Borr Drilling. Meanwhile, the drillship’s sister vessel, Noble Globetrotter I , has secured fresh employment with Occidental offshore Peru, starting in the second quarter of 2027 at a dayrate of $400,000. The rig is subsequently expected to begin a three-year light well intervention arrangement with TotalEnergies in West Africa, with a minimum commitment of 150 days annually. Noble reported a contracted backlog of $6.7bn as of October 26, following approximately $560m in new awards since its previous fleet status update. articles.title: Norway lines up full-scale test of marine nuclear propulsion system
articles.summary: A Norwegian-led consortium involving shipbuilder Vard and offshore vessel owner Island Offshore is preparing to build and test an integrated nuclear propulsion system, targeting its first vessel deployment in 2031 or 2032. The Marine Nuclear Propulsion System (MarNuPS) project, led by Emerald Nuclear Norway, will...
articles.body: Europe Offshore Norway lines up full-scale test of marine nuclear propulsion system Bojan Lepic October 28, 2026 0 1,649 1 minute read A Norwegian-led consortium involving shipbuilder Vard and offshore vessel owner Island Offshore is preparing to build and test an integrated nuclear propulsion system, targeting its first vessel deployment in 2031 or 2032. The Marine Nuclear Propulsion System (MarNuPS) project, led by Emerald Nuclear Norway, will move from engineering studies to physical integration and testing, with a full-scale test facility planned at Stette near Ålesund in 2027. The project will combine Emerald Nuclear’s 5 MW electric Gem microreactor technology with energy storage, power conversion, vessel power management, automation and bridge control systems. The initial testing phase will use electric heating instead of nuclear fuel to simulate reactor operation, allowing engineers to assess how the propulsion system performs under realistic vessel operating conditions. Tests will examine normal operation, rapid changes in power demand, system stress, emergency responses and interaction with ship crews. The consortium includes Vard Group, Vard Electro, Island Offshore, the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU), Imperial College London and engineering specialist Maskindynamikk. Vard will handle ship design and integration, while Vard Electro will develop power management and automation systems. Island Offshore will contribute operational expertise and plans to become the first shipowner to install the technology on an offshore vessel. The initiative builds on the NTNU-led NuProShip research programme, which has been examining the feasibility of integrating advanced nuclear reactors into commercial shipping. Earlier this year, Vard presented a nuclear-powered offshore construction vessel concept developed through NuProShip II, examining reactor integration, operational requirements and safety considerations. The latest pilot has received NOK20m ($2m) from the Research Council of Norway, while its initial development stage is expected to cost approximately NOK150m ($15.6m), including partner contributions. Although the project is targeting commercial demonstration early in the next decade, actual vessel deployment will depend on completing technical qualification and obtaining the necessary regulatory approvals. articles.title: Europe’s container ports: Why is transshipment falling while gateway traffic grows?
articles.summary: Europe’s major container ports are reporting increasingly contrasting traffic patterns in 2026, with headline throughput figures concealing significant changes in the composition of cargo flows. At Rotterdam and Valencia, transshipment volumes have declined substantially during the first nine months of the year,...
articles.body: Europe’s major container ports are reporting increasingly contrasting traffic patterns in 2026, with headline throughput figures concealing significant changes in the composition of cargo flows. At Rotterdam and Valencia, transshipment volumes have declined substantially during the first nine months of the year, while traffic linked to imports and inland markets has strengthened. Antwerp-Bruges presents a different picture, with modest overall container growth driven by empty rather than full containers. The figures raise an important question for Europe’s port sector: are changes in terminal capacity, cargo demand and shipping networks altering the balance between transshipment and gateway activity? The available evidence points to changes at individual ports rather than a confirmed Europe-wide shift. Rotterdam: Terminal capacity reshapes cargo flows According to the Port of Rotterdam Authority’s nine-month results , container throughput increased by just 0.1% in TEUs during January–September 2026, while containerised cargo measured in tonnes declined by 2.2%. Behind the relatively stable headline figure, however, two sharply different trends emerged. Transshipment throughput fell by 20%, while hinterland container volumes increased by 7.2%. Full-container imports serving inland markets rose by 8.9%, compared with growth of just 1% in full-container exports. The explanation provided by the port authority is particularly significant. Long-standing capacity constraints at Rotterdam’s deep-sea terminals have resulted in more cargo being handled through alternative ports, freeing capacity for containers moving to and from the hinterland. This suggests that Rotterdam’s changing cargo mix cannot be attributed solely to shifts in underlying demand. Terminal capacity and operational constraints are also influencing which cargo flows remain within the port. As Container News reported , the decline in transshipment has occurred alongside continued growth in inland-linked traffic. For terminal operators and shipping lines, the distinction matters. Transshipment containers depend heavily on vessel connections and network design, whereas gateway cargo also relies on inland distribution infrastructure and access to regional markets. Rotterdam’s results therefore illustrate how operational limitations can influence the balance between these activities without producing a comparable decline in total TEUs. Valencia: Stronger imports, weaker transshipment Valencia is experiencing a similar divergence in traffic categories, although the available figures do not establish the same underlying cause. According to Valenciaport’s September traffic report , total container throughput declined by 0.91% during the first nine months of 2026, reaching approximately 4.2 million TEUs. Full-container imports increased by 10.02% to 856,431 TEUs, while full-container exports rose marginally by 0.31% to 681,113 TEUs. In contrast, full containers handled in transshipment fell by 9.81% to 1,552,065 units. The difference is substantial. Valencia is recording stronger inbound container activity while losing volume in a segment that remains central to its position within Mediterranean shipping networks. However, the latest monthly figures introduce an important qualification. During September alone, full-container transshipment declined by just 0.82%, a considerably smaller reduction than the cumulative nine-month figure. Meanwhile, full-container imports increased by 11.68% and exports by 5.68%. As highlighted in Container News’ coverage of Valenciaport’s latest results , September’s performance suggests that the earlier decline in transshipment was moderating. This makes it premature to describe Valencia’s weaker transshipment performance as a permanent structural change. Unlike Rotterdam, where the port authority explicitly identified terminal capacity constraints, Valencia’s published figures do not establish a single comparable explanation for the reduction. Antwerp-Bruges: More TEUs do not necessarily mean more full containers The Port of Antwerp-Bruges’ nine-month results provide a third perspective on Europe’s changing container traffic. Total container throughput increased by 1.2% in TEUs, supported by a strong recovery during the third quarter. Yet full-container throughput declined by 1.3%, while empty-container movements increased by 11.7%. The port authority linked this development to rising import volumes and pressure on exports, which increased the need to reposition empty equipment, particularly towards Asia. This distinction demonstrates why total TEU growth cannot automatically be interpreted as an equivalent increase in laden cargo activity. A port can report higher container volumes while handling fewer full containers, depending on the balance between imports, exports and empty-equipment movements. Antwerp-Bruges also illustrates a limitation of direct port comparisons. Its published nine-month figures do not provide the same transshipment breakdown available for Rotterdam and Valencia. Consequently, its performance is useful for understanding the changing composition of European container traffic, but not for establishing whether transshipment is declining across the region. What the differences mean for European port competition Taken together, the three ports reveal a more complex picture than their aggregate throughput growth rates suggest. Rotterdam’s transshipment decline is explicitly associated with deep-sea terminal capacity constraints. Valencia combines weaker cumulative transshipment with stronger imports and a recent moderation in the decline. Antwerp-Bruges shows how empty-container repositioning can support overall TEU growth even as full-container traffic contracts. These developments also highlight the importance of distinguishing actual container movements from the nominal vessel capacity deployed by shipping lines. Changes in service rotations and port calls may influence future traffic distribution, but announced network capacity cannot be treated as evidence of equivalent cargo volumes. For European ports, the competitive implications will depend on whether current changes persist, how terminal capacity develops and whether shipping lines continue adjusting their networks. The next reporting periods will be particularly important for Valencia, where September’s figures suggest improving transshipment performance, and for Rotterdam, where capacity constraints remain a documented factor. The central finding is not that Europe’s ports are collectively moving away from transshipment. It is that the relationship between transshipment, gateway cargo and total container throughput is becoming increasingly important to understanding their individual performance.
takeaways: Europe’s major container ports are reporting increasingly contrasting traffic patterns in 2026, with headline throughput figures concealing significant changes in the composition of cargo flows.
At Rotterdam and Valencia, transshipment volumes have declined substantially during the first nine months of the year, while traffic linked to imports and inland markets has strengthened.
Antwerp-Bruges presents a different picture, with modest overall container growth driven by empty rather than full containers.

HJ Heavy Industries, J-Ocean Heavy Industries, Myeongun Industrial Development and turbine manufacturer Unison signed a memorandum of understanding to develop the facility on South Korea’s western coast. The project will use about 330,000 sq m of unused shipyard land to establish a manufacturing cluster to serve the country’s expanding offshore wind industry. HJ Heavy Industries will contribute its shipbuilding and offshore engineering expertise to establish production capabilities for turbine towers, offshore substations and other structures. J-Ocean Heavy Industries will provide shipyard infrastructure and manufacturing facilities, while Myeongun Industrial Development will contribute offshore wind project development expertise. The planned manufacturing hub already has a potential customer in Myeongun’s 340MW Hanbit offshore wind project. Unison intends to manufacture 25 turbines rated at 13.6 MW for the project, planned off South Korea’s southwest coast. The Hanbit project is targeting construction from July 2027, with completion scheduled for December 2029. The proposed Gunsan facility is part of Unison’s broader plan to build annual turbine manufacturing capacity of 1GW. The initiative aims to build a domestic supply chain for large offshore wind equipment as South Korea pursues its target of 25GW of installed offshore wind capacity by 2035. The agreement could bring one of the region’s largest undeveloped offshore gas resources under full Timorese ownership, following a separate agreement for TIMOR GAP to acquire Japanese company Osaka Gas’s 10% interest. Under the latest transaction, TIMOR GAP will pay Woodside $13.71m upon completion, with another $11.29m due following a final investment decision. The Sunrise and Troubadour fields, collectively known as Greater Sunrise, lie approximately 150 km southeast of Timor-Leste and 450 km northwest of Darwin. The development is estimated to contain 5.1trn cubic feet of gas and 226m barrels of condensate. TIMOR GAP intends to advance a development concept involving a pipeline to Natarbora on Timor-Leste’s southern coast, supporting the country’s long-standing ambition to establish a domestic LNG industry. The project has remained undeveloped for decades amid disagreements over processing-facility locations and the commercial viability of competing development concepts. TIMOR GAP chief executive Rui Soares said consolidating ownership would help accelerate project development and advance selection of the Timor LNG concept. Woodside chief executive Liz Westcott added that the sale reflected the company’s approach to portfolio management and capital allocation. articles.title: Containership orderbook heads towards 16m teu
articles.summary: The containership industry’s extraordinary ordering spree is showing no signs of slowing, with the global orderbook now exceeding 15m teu and another wave of megamax contracts poised to push the total towards 16m teu before the end of the year.
