articles.body: Containers Operations Containership orderbook heads towards 16m teu Sam Chambers October 28, 2026 0 1,381 2 minutes read The containership industry’s extraordinary ordering spree is showing no signs of slowing, with the global orderbook now exceeding 15m teu and another wave of megamax contracts poised to push the total towards 16m teu before the end of the year. The latest figures from Alphaliner show that approximately 40 additional large containerships are expected to join the newbuilding pipeline, involving Maersk, Yang Ming, CMA CGM and MSC. Orders from the first two carriers are expected shortly, while contracts involving CMA CGM and MSC are believed to have been signed but have yet to be confirmed by Alphaliner. Among the most significant prospective deals is Maersk’s return to the largest containership segment. Alphaliner reports that the Danish carrier is negotiating exclusively with Chinese shipyards for a series of twelve LNG dual-fuel vessels of 24,000 teu, potentially accompanied by options for another twelve. At an estimated $240m apiece, the initial programme would be worth approximately $2.88bn, rising to $5.76bn if all options were exercised. The ships would represent Maersk’s first entry into the 24,000 teu category, moving beyond the distinctive twin-engine Triple-E designs it introduced more than a decade ago. Chinese yards are being favoured on cost and available construction slots. The orderbook’s expansion is particularly striking against the size of the existing fleet. Alphaliner’s October Monthly Monitor put contracted capacity at 15.12m teu, equivalent to 43.9% of the trading fleet. Its projections show fleet capacity expanding by 9.2% in 2027 and a further 14.4% in 2028. That supply wave is arriving just as the industry’s operating geography undergoes another fundamental change. Sea-Intelligence reported this week that around 60% of deployed Asia-Europe capacity is now operating, or scheduled to operate, via Suez rather than around the Cape of Good Hope. Assuming security conditions permit, the consultancy expects further normalisation during the first quarter of 2027. Returning to shorter voyages will release effective vessel capacity into a market already facing accelerating physical deliveries. Braemar warned in its latest container briefing that the combination of returning Suez services and the expanding orderbook was “not an ideal combination for charter rates”. Jefferies has expressed similar caution over 2027, warning that newbuilding deliveries could push fleet growth ahead of cargo demand. Yet today’s charter market remains remarkably resilient. Alphaliner reports that only 0.8% of the global cellular fleet was commercially idle in its latest survey, while charter rates have climbed to their highest levels in four years. Promptly available ships remain exceptionally scarce, with some large units reportedly commanding six-figure daily earnings. The ordering boom is also reshaping propulsion choices. LNG dual-fuel ships now represent 56% of contracted capacity, compared with 12% for methanol dual-fuel vessels. Conventional propulsion accounts for just under 32%. Alphaliner recorded 2.3m teu of fresh LNG dual-fuel orders during 2026, with the anticipated megamax contracts potentially adding another 1m teu. Methanol ordering, by contrast, has almost stalled. For now, geopolitical disruption and tight prompt vessel availability continue to underpin exceptional charter earnings. But Alphaliner cautioned that the coming delivery avalanche “will eventually take its toll on the market”. articles.title: Maritime CEO Forum: Shipping’s wartime boom tests discipline
articles.summary: Shipping may be enjoying one of its strongest booms in decades, but the extraordinary profits generated by geopolitical turmoil are raising difficult questions about risk, investment and what happens when the wars end, delegates at yesterday’s Maritime CEO Forum in Monaco heard. Opening the event at the Yacht Club de...
articles.body: Europe Maritime CEO Operations Maritime CEO Forum: Shipping’s wartime boom tests discipline Splash October 28, 2026 0 578 2 minutes read Splash Splash Shipping may be enjoying one of its strongest booms in decades, but the extraordinary profits generated by geopolitical turmoil are raising difficult questions about risk, investment and what happens when the wars end, delegates at yesterday’s Maritime CEO Forum in Monaco heard. Opening the event at the Yacht Club de Monaco, Splash editor Sam Chambers asked whether today’s riches were encouraging owners to repeat the mistakes of past cycles. Burak Cetinok, head of research at Arrow, described the rally as unusually broad across freight, vessel values and sale-and-purchase activity. VLCC earnings this month were 14 times their 10-year average, he calculated, with the weekly multiple approaching 20. The latest peak was four times that of 2007-08. Despite the eye-watering numbers, Cetinok saw no immediate sell signal in conventional shipping. His biggest concern was fresh capacity: Arrow’s analysis suggested that once an orderbook reaches roughly 25% of the existing fleet, earnings have historically tended to fall within 24 to 36 months. Svein Moxnes Harfjeld, chief executive of DHT Holdings, was more sanguine about the VLCC orderbook. By the end of 2029, he said, almost half the fleet would be over 15 years old and a quarter over 20, creating considerable replacement demand. With tanker owners generally carrying much less debt than before the 2008 crash, he argued, the industry was also more resilient. For DHT, avoiding boom-time exuberance meant sticking to internal “traffic lights” governing investment and risk, even when high spot rates made restraint look costly. Illustrating the desperation to secure oil supplies, Harfjeld described a refinery customer accepting a voyage 40 days longer, at a 50% higher freight rate, to avoid heightened Red Sea risks. Gus Majed, founder and group chief executive of Paratus, said the surge in tanker earnings was a rational response to the breakdown of established energy routes and refining markets. But the frequency of attacks was making returns less attractive after adjusting for risk. “Returns are starting to compress on a risk-adjusted basis,” he said, warning that governments and companies were reassessing energy security and strategic stockpiles. A flattening between spot and forward freight rates would be one sign that the boom was losing momentum. René Kofod-Olsen, chief executive of V.Group, warned that record earnings should not obscure operational vulnerabilities. Some owners were still managing fleets of “10, 20, 30 ships on WhatsApp and the occasional e-mail”, he said, while cyberattacks on vessels and offices underscored the need for investment in systems and training. Above all, he urged owners not to treat seafarers and technical management as commodities. From the floor, Andy Dacy of JP Morgan Asset Management cautioned against chasing ships at the top of the market and suggested public and private owners might react differently when valuations turned. Another delegate, Lars-Christian Svensen, who heads Bruton, Himalaya Shipping and OMC Tankers, countered that flexibility mattered more than identifying as a spot or long-term player. Owners needed to be nimble and prepared to sell into strength. Tomorrow, Splash will bring readers details from yesterday’s tanker session at the exclusive shipowner gathering on the Cote d’Azur. Russian deputy prime minister Alexander Novak confirmed yesterday that three shipments were underway, despite mounting opposition from US lawmakers who argue the deal breaches existing legislation prohibiting Russian energy imports. According to vessel tracking data from Kpler, the ships are Talisman, Leruo and Agioi Fanendes, carrying a combined 924,000 barrels of diesel. The three ships departed Primorsk between October 16 and 22 and are expected to reach the US Atlantic coast between November 7 and 11, although their declared destinations remain subject to change. Novak said the shipments demonstrate that Moscow and Washington are implementing their agreement despite political opposition. The Trump administration issued a six-month sanctions exemption earlier this month, allowing transactions involving Russian-origin diesel until April 7 next year. The concession is intended to help alleviate soaring US fuel prices, which have been driven higher by the Iran conflict and disruptions to global refining and shipping. However, the agreement has created a legal and political confrontation. A bipartisan group of US lawmakers has warned banks, ports and energy companies against handling the cargoes, arguing that the Treasury exemption cannot override legislation passed in 2022 banning imports of Russian petroleum products. articles.body: UPS reported higher third-quarter revenue across its domestic, international and supply chain businesses. The logistics group also raised its financial guidance for the fourth quarter and full year. Consolidated revenue increased by 6.7% to US$22.9 billion. Operating profit reached US$1.7 billion, while adjusted operating profit was US$2.1 billion. UPS reported diluted earnings of US$1.37 per share. Adjusted diluted earnings stood at US$1.69 per share. The reported results included a net charge of US$279 million. This comprised transformation costs and a goodwill impairment charge in Supply Chain Solutions, partly offset by a gain from the sale of MD-11 assets. “Our third-quarter results demonstrate the continued strengthening of our business fundamentals, driven by premium growth and greater network efficiency,” said Carol Tomé, Chief Executive Officer of UPS. Revenue rises across all divisions Revenue in the US Domestic segment increased by 4.5% to US$14.87 billion. The improvement was driven by a 6.1% increase in revenue per piece. The segment generated operating profit of US$906 million and adjusted operating profit of US$1.03 billion. Its reported operating margin was 6.1%, while the adjusted margin reached 7%. International revenue increased by 7.1% to slightly above US$5 billion. Revenue per piece rose by 15%, while operating profit reached US$746 million. The International segment achieved an operating margin of 14.9% on both a reported and adjusted basis. Forwarding and logistics support supply chain growth Supply Chain Solutions revenue increased by 18.2% to US$2.98 billion. UPS attributed the growth mainly to its forwarding and logistics operations, including healthcare logistics. Reported operating profit declined to US$92 million. However, adjusted operating profit reached US$274 million, compared with US$536 million in the same period of 2025. The segment recorded a reported operating margin of 3.1% and an adjusted margin of 9.2%. UPS raises 2026 guidance UPS now expects fourth-quarter revenue of approximately US$25.7 billion. Adjusted operating profit is forecast at around US$3.3 billion. For the full year, the company expects consolidated revenue of approximately US$92.6 billion. It also forecasts adjusted operating profit of US$8.75 billion and adjusted diluted earnings of US$7.28 per share. UPS raised its adjusted free cash flow target to approximately US$6.1 billion. It maintained its expectations for capital expenditure of US$3 billion and dividend payments of around US$5.4 billion, subject to board approval.

articles.body: Port Everglades in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, welcomed more than 5.38 million cruise passengers during fiscal year 2026, setting a new annual record for the third consecutive year. The latest figures reflect continued growth in the port’s cruise operations as it prepares for another season with additional vessels, upgraded facilities and expanded passenger services. The port expects to host nine cruise lines and 40 cruise ships during the new season. Participating operators include Royal Caribbean, Celebrity Cruises, Disney Cruise Line, Princess Cruises, Holland America Line, Cunard, Crystal, Viking Ocean Cruises and Orient Express Sailing Yachts. The upcoming schedule also includes several new additions to the port’s homeporting operations. Royal Caribbean’s Legend of the Seas , an Icon-class cruise ship with capacity for up to 7,600 guests, is scheduled to arrive in November and homeport at Port Everglades for the 2027 season. Meanwhile, the newbuild Orient Express Corinthian will join the port’s cruise programme, alongside Crystal’s refurbished Crystal Symphony , which accommodates 606 guests. Port Everglades upgrades cruise infrastructure Alongside its passenger growth, Port Everglades has completed improvements to Cruise Terminal 18, which originally opened in 2009. The terminal has received a refreshed exterior, redesigned embarkation areas and additional passenger facilities. Improvements include more open interior spaces, new furniture and updated artwork in the VIP lounge. The port has also expanded parking capacity near the terminal. More than 850 spaces have been added, bringing the total number of available parking spaces across its garages and parking areas to 6,386. These upgrades are intended to support passenger operations as cruise activity continues to expand. New leadership for cruise operations Port Everglades has also appointed Martin Jackson as Director of its newly established Cruise Services Division. Jackson previously served as Assistant Director of the Cruise Services Section and joined the port in January 2025. The appointment follows approval of the fiscal year 2027 budget by the Broward County Board of County Commissioners. According to Joseph Morris, CEO and Port Director of Port Everglades, the organisational changes are designed to maintain service standards while supporting future growth. “Operational consistency earns trust, both internally and with our guests and customers, while continuous improvement ensures we are always making progress and moving ideas, vision, and strategy forward,” said Martin Jackson, Director of the Cruise Services Division at Port Everglades. The port has also released its 2027–2028 Cruise Guide, outlining upcoming sailings and itineraries for the new season.

articles.title: US revises tariffs on Canadian goods ahead of October 30 changes
articles.summary: The United States has announced changes to its 50% tariffs on selected Canadian products, removing certain goods from the existing measures while adding new product categories. The modifications were introduced through a presidential proclamation signed on October 23, 2026, under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of...
articles.body: The United States has announced changes to its 50% tariffs on selected Canadian products , removing certain goods from the existing measures while adding new product categories. The modifications were introduced through a presidential proclamation signed on October 23, 2026, under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930. They will take effect on October 30, changing the tariff treatment of a range of Canadian goods entering the US market. The latest measures amend tariffs introduced in July and subsequently modified in September, reflecting another adjustment to trade restrictions between the two countries. Changes to products covered by US tariffs Under the revised measures, several Canadian products will no longer be subject to the additional 50% Section 338 duties. The exemptions include certain plywood sheets, paper and paperboard products, packaging materials, and selected industrial machinery and refrigeration equipment. According to a trade update published by Expeditors, other affected products include certain seaweeds and algae, along with non-adhesive sheets, films and foils made from polypropylene. At the same time, the US administration is expanding the list of goods covered by the additional duties. More than 100 products are being added, including certain paints, soaps, artificial waxes, vinyl flooring, fiberboard, carpets and industrial materials. The changes affect specific tariff classifications rather than all products within these broader categories. For importers and logistics providers, the revised product coverage will require attention to the applicable Harmonized Tariff Schedule classifications when arranging shipments and customs clearance. New tariff rules take effect on October 30 The White House confirmed that the changes will apply to covered goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouses for consumption, from 12:01 a.m. Eastern Time on October 30, 2026. The administration also clarified that the additional Section 338 tariffs apply to covered Canadian goods regardless of whether they qualify as originating goods under the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA). Furthermore, the measures may apply in addition to duties imposed under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962. The presidential proclamation authorises US Customs and Border Protection to issue the instructions and regulatory guidance necessary to implement the changes. The latest adjustments follow earlier modifications to the Section 338 measures in September, as the US administration continues to revise the scope of tariffs affecting Canadian exports. For companies involved in cross-border trade, the October 30 implementation date marks another change in the customs treatment of selected Canadian products.

articles.body: VLCC transits climb at Hormuz; steady at Bab al-Mandab for second day in International Shipping News 28/10/2026 The Strait of Hormuz had six VLCC transits on Oct. 25, the most since Oct. 17, while the Bab al-Mandab Strait recorded one VLCC on both Oct. 24 and Oct. 25, S&P Global Commodities at Sea said in an Oct. 26 report. Hormuz traffic in total was steady at 17 ships on Oct. 24 and Oct. 25, while Bab al-Mandab transits jumped to 42 ships from 27 ships over the same period, according to the CAS report. The VLCC total for Hormuz on Oct. 25 was up from five on Oct. 24, CAS data showed. The outbound VLCC from the Persian Gulf was Monaco Prosperity, while inbound VLCCs were Bangladesh Prosperity, Ennie, Thailand Prosperity, West Loyalty and Bulgaria Prosperity, CAS said. The VLCCs that transited Bab al-Mandab were Della, heading northbound, on Oct. 25 and Karina, also moving northbound, on Oct. 24, according to CAS. US forces on Oct. 25 marked the export of at least 1.5 billion barrels of crude oil since the summer through Hormuz, with US Central Command commander Admiral Brad Cooper flying over the chokepoint in a US Army CH-47 Chinook, Central Command said on X. It noted that more than 3,000 commercial ships had successfully transited Hormuz with support from CENTCOM forces over the last six months. “Today, primary transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz remain free and clear of Iranian sea mines thanks to incredible efforts by our people,” Cooper said. “We remain intensely focused on keeping commercial traffic flowing as we work with our teammates in the US interagency, Gulf Cooperation Council, and shipping industry.” The comment came despite Iran launching its heaviest wave of attacks on merchant ships around Hormuz and in the wider region this month, with the International Maritime Organization recording 29 attacks during Oct. 1-22, exceeding all monthly tallies since March. On Oct. 26, the UK Maritime Trade Operations Centre reported a tanker exiting Hormuz was disabled after being struck by an unknown projectile Oct. 23. No crew casualties or oil spills have been reported. Of the 16 VLCC crossings identified over Oct. 23-25, 10 were assessed as inbound and six outbound, CAS said. Inbound VLCC movements included five of South Korea’s Sinokor-operated ships, and the Saudi-linked Majra and Qasba. The VLCC Ennie moved into the Persian Gulf after last loading a cargo of Basrah Heavy crude in early October, and China-owned VLCC Indigo Ray also moved inbound, CAS said. Outbound transits included Sinokor-operated Romania Prosperity, UAE-linked Das and Al Faya, and Saudi-linked Kahla and Emerald Shine, CAS said. LPG tankers Over Oct. 23-25, five LPG tankers were observed crossing the Strait of Hormuz, including one outbound and four inbound transits, CAS said. The outbound ship was the Marshall Islands-flagged Very Large Gas Carrier Sheng Hai Long, which had been in the Persian Gulf since Aug. 21, CAS said. During its stay, the ship loaded LPG at Ras Laffan, Qatar, while operating without AIS visibility, then exited the strait in a dark transit before reappearing in the Arabian Sea on Oct. 24, CAS said. On Oct. 24, two LPG tankers entered the Gulf. One was UAE-linked Sweihan, which previously transferred cargo at Vadinar, India, and was last seen heading for Ruwais, UAE, for its next loading, CAS said. On Oct. 25, UAE-linked LPG tanker Delma was last seen berthed at Ras Laffan for loading, CAS said. Activity across the US naval blockade line came to 57 transits on Oct. 25, up from 51 on Oct. 24, according to CAS. Source: Platts 2026-10-28 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.summary: A new market development for tankers could be shaping up, after the latest agreement between US and Russia, regarding diesel exports across the Atlantic. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Xclusiv said that “the latest developments in US–Russian energy relations could mark another turning point for the product...
articles.body: Russian Diesel Returns: A New Atlantic Trade Dynamic in Hellenic Shipping News 28/10/2026 A new market development for tankers could be shaping up, after the latest agreement between US and Russia, regarding diesel exports across the Atlantic. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Xclusiv said that “the latest developments in US–Russian energy relations could mark another turning point for the product tanker market, as Washington’s decision to temporarily ease sanctions on Russian diesel opens the door to renewed trade flows between two countries whose energy relationship has been severely restricted since 2022. According to Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, the first diesel cargo of approximately 40,000 mt is scheduled to depart Russia’s Baltic coast on October 22, with Moscow targeting 300,000 mt of shipments to the US during October and a further 500,000 mt in November. Beyond the political significance, this development raises important questions regarding Atlantic product tanker demand, vessel availability and the potential redistribution of established trading patterns”. Source: Xclusiv shipbroker According to Xclusiv, “interestingly, maritime trade in petroleum products between Russia and the US has diminished significantly following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, but has never completely disappeared. On 2020 and 2021 the seaborne trade of oil products from Russia to USA was around 23 million mt annually. Based on Signal Ocean data, during 2023, recorded shipments reached approximately 1.33 million mt, declining to 1.06 million mt in 2024, before recovering to 1.28 million mt in 2025. During January–June 2026, volumes totalled 510,000 mt, compared to 727,000 mt during the corresponding period of 2025, representing a contraction of almost 30%. July recorded no shipments, highlighting the weakening momentum before the latest diplomatic developments. These figures suggest that the announced reopening should be viewed not simply as the restoration of previously interrupted trade, but as a potential expansion and restructuring of existing flows, particularly concerning diesel”. The shipbroker added that “from a shipping perspective, the implications could be particularly interesting for the MR segment. The initial 40,000 mt cargo fits comfortably within MR2 employment, while the proposed 500,000 mt November programme could theoretically generate around 10–13 MR-sized cargoes, depending on parcel sizes. More importantly, shipments from Russia’s Baltic terminals towards the US Atlantic coast would introduce additional employment opportunities into a market already experiencing significant volatility. However, the actual benefit will depend on whether these shipments represent genuinely additional demand or simply replace diesel currently sourced from Northwest Europe, Canada and South Korea. In the latter case, the redistribution of existing cargoes could still reshape vessel positioning and regional freight differentials. Another important consideration is the current competition between clean and dirty tanker markets. With crude tanker earnings remaining exceptionally attractive, several LR vessels have shifted towards crude transportation, reducing the effective availability of tonnage dedicated to refined products. Returning these vessels to clean trading is neither immediate nor straightforward, as tank cleaning and preparation require additional time and costs. Consequently, renewed Russian diesel movements could arrive at a particularly favourable moment for MR owners, especially if increased Atlantic demand coincides with limited LR participation in the clean market”. Source: Xclusiv shipbroker “Nevertheless, Russia’s ability to deliver the announced volumes remains uncertain. Ukrainian attacks against Russian refineries have constrained production and export capacity, while Moscow’s own restrictions on diesel exports underline the importance of protecting domestic supply. Although Novak anticipates a recovery towards the country’s traditional 3.5 million mt monthly diesel export capacity by year-end, actual shipments will depend heavily on refinery operations and logistical availability. Ultimately, the significance of this agreement extends beyond the initial cargoes. With gasoil prices remaining elevated and geopolitical disruptions continuing to reshape energy flows, even relatively modest changes in trade policy can influence vessel utilisation and freight sentiment. For product tanker owners, the key question is whether this reopening develops into a sustained Atlantic trade corridor. Should Russian export capacity recover while LR vessels remain attracted to the crude market, MR tankers could emerge as important beneficiaries of another geopolitical reshuffling of global petroleum trade”, Xclusiv concluded. articles.title: Maritime industry advances harmonisation of digital emissions reporting
articles.summary: The Tripartite Joint Industry Working Group (JIWG) has released two new frameworks that can help improve the exchange of operations and emissions data across the maritime industry. The JIWG, chaired by BIMCO, was established under the Tripartite, a forum bringing together shipowners and operators, shipbuilders, and...
articles.body: Maritime industry advances harmonisation of digital emissions reporting in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 28/10/2026 T he Tripartite Joint Industry Working Group (JIWG) has released two new frameworks that can help improve the exchange of operations and emissions data across the maritime industry. The JIWG, chaired by BIMCO, was established under the Tripartite, a forum bringing together shipowners and operators, shipbuilders, and classification societies. As part of its work to develop a common approach for Maritime Emissions Reporting, the JIWG has released version 1.0 of the Operational Vessel Data (OVD) and Vessel Emissions Reporting (VER) frameworks. The two frameworks complement each other and can help establish a common foundation for a more efficient exchange of data. Both OVD and VER are voluntary industry frameworks. They do not create new reporting obligations but provide a common approach that organisations may adopt to support more efficient and consistent data exchange. The JIWG’s development of the OVD and VER frameworks complements and builds on earlier work by BIMCO and IACS (International Association of Classification Societies) to add emissions-reporting data elements to the IMO Compendium on Facilitation and Electronic Business. While the IMO Compendium provides common definitions and formats for maritime information, the latest work adds a practical implementation framework for exchanging operational vessel data and verified emissions-reporting results between industry systems. The initiative also forms part of a broader move towards using the IMO Compendium as a common foundation for maritime data exchange. Emerging use cases covering port-call optimisation, electronic seafarer certificates and maritime emissions reporting demonstrate how common data definitions can support interoperability across different parts of the maritime sector. The work of the group addresses the common industry challenge of stakeholders facing different reporting systems and data formats which often result in the same information being mapped, entered and checked multiple times. The OVD and VER can support a more consistent, efficient and traceable exchange of data between ships, shipping companies, software providers, verification bodies and other authorised users. The approach will also make it easier to reuse data more consistently across the industry and connected value chains. Two complementary parts of the data flow The OVD provides a structured format for exchanging operational vessel and fuel-consumption data. It defines common data elements, names, units and structures, allowing the information to be interpreted consistently by different systems and organisations. It does not prescribe how data must be collected onboard, which software must be used or where data must be stored, but instead provides a common approach for sharing such data across the maritime industry. The VER complements the OVD by providing standardised formats for emissions reporting in cases when commercial reporting practices and needs vary considerably. This could include charter-party performance, Emission Trading Schemes (ETS) cost allocation, FuelEU pooling and other commercial arrangements. The VER provides a common way to exchange emissions information, including its verification status for reporting periods that are defined by the user. In practical terms, the OVD provides the underlying operational data layer while the VER provides a structured output solution for emissions information. In combination, the two solutions can help support the maritime industry’s objective of capturing data only once and reusing it for all relevant reporting, verification and other purposes. See also the illustration in the annex, which shows the exchange of operational and emissions data across the maritime industry. Responding to a growing reporting burden The need for accurate and trusted maritime emissions reporting has increased due to the IMO Data Collection System (IMO DCS) and the EU Monitoring, Reporting and Verification system (EU MRV). Although these requirements serve different purposes, the use of different datasets and system formats can create inconsistencies, repeated data mapping and manual work across the reporting chain. The Tripartite JIWG has therefore worked to develop a common approach that allows data to move between different systems, regardless of the technology or service provider used. The OVD builds on a framework initially developed by DNV and subsequently considered through the wider JIWG process. The VER builds on an initial draft prepared by ClassNK and was further developed collaboratively by the participating organisations. Industry collaboration and practical implementation As voluntary industry frameworks, OVD and VER version 1.0 provides a baseline for practical use and further development. Organisations can now consider how the formats may be applied within existing systems and processes. Experience from implementation and real-world use will help identify where definitions, guidance, tools or data structures may need further refinement. Illustration of the exchange of operational and emissions data across the maritime As part of the next phase, the Tripartite Joint Industry Working Group will also assess options for transitioning OVD and VER towards independent and broadly representative governance. The objective is to establish clear ownership, open participation, transparent decision-making and predictable change management, providing confidence that the frameworks can be maintained as neutral and accessible industry resources. The Joint Industry Working Group will continue to oversee the work while the governance alternatives are assessed and until an appropriate structure is ready to receive the frameworks. No final governance model has yet been selected. Quotes Yasuhiro Ikeda, Director, Digital Solutions Division, ClassNK “VER is the result of a truly collaborative effort across all participating organisations, and I would like to thank everyone who contributed to this achievement. By establishing a common foundation for trusted and interoperable emissions data exchange, VER will help improve efficiency, transparency and digital collaboration across the maritime industry. Version 1.0 marks an important beginning, and we look forward to expanding its value through practical use and continued industry cooperation.” Bjarte Walaker, Head of Maritime Deliveries, Veracity by DNV “After several years of developing OVD, DNV is very pleased to see its broad adoption and grateful to the shipping companies, solution providers and other contributors who have helped turn it into a formal industry standard. This shared commitment is essential to enabling more efficient, consistent and interoperable exchange of vessel data, helping to reduce friction and support innovation across the maritime industry and connected value chains.” Vincent Joly, Smartship Manager – Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore “As reporting requirements continue to evolve, greater alignment in operational and emissions data is becoming increasingly important. Bureau Veritas has already adopted OVD for emissions data collection and supports this industry-led effort to establish common approaches for data exchange. These frameworks provide an important foundation for greater consistency across reporting and verification activities, enabling information to be shared and used more effectively across the maritime ecosystem.” Michela Schenone, Marine Digital and Class Solutions Operations Director – RINA “RINA believes that common industry standards are essential to make maritime emissions reporting more efficient, consistent and interoperable. RINA is taking practical steps to adopt OVD within its emissions reporting processes, supporting a common approach to data exchange across the industry. Continued industry collaboration will be key to achieving broad adoption and ensuring that these common frameworks deliver long-lasting value across the maritime sector.” Jeppe Skovbakke Juhl, Chief Naval Architect, Regulatory Affairs, BIMCO – chair of the JIWG “The maritime industry does not need more ways of exchanging the same information. It needs a common approach that allows data to move efficiently between organisations and systems. OVD and VER are an important step in that direction, reducing duplication and creating a stronger foundation for efficient and interoperable reporting.” Source: Tripartite Joint Industry Working Group Tops 2026-10-28 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: The JIWG, chaired by BIMCO, was established under the Tripartite, a forum bringing together shipowners and operators, shipbuilders, and classification societies.

As part of its work to develop a common approach for Maritime Emissions Reporting, the JIWG has released version 1.0 of the Operational Vessel Data (OVD) and Vessel Emissions Reporting (VER) frameworks.
The two frameworks complement each other and can help establish a common foundation for a more efficient exchange of data.

articles.summary: The International Union of Marine Insurance (IUMI) has, today, released its 2026 analysis of the global marine insurance market – the IUMI “Stats Report”. articles.body: IUMI’s annual Stats Report highlights modest market development amid continued soft conditions across all main business lines in Marine Insurance P&I Club News 28/10/2026 T he International Union of Marine Insurance (IUMI) has, today, released its 2026 analysis of the global marine insurance market – the IUMI “Stats Report”. This annual document reports on the state of the marine insurance sector within the framework of the global economy, trade and shipping. Data is collected from a wide range of national insurance associations and other agencies including IUMI’s own sources and is collated, analysed and presented with additional context and commentary. Highlights from this year’s report includes: • Global marine insurance premiums reached USD 42.6 billion in 2025, up 5.5 percent on 2024. However, US dollar weakness masked any underlying market development while increased capacity and competition continued to drive soft market conditions. • Marine cargo premiums were reported as USD 24.2 billion, up 6.9 percent year-on-year, supported by seaborne trade and asset and commodity price movements. Chinese premiums continued to grow strongly, driven by high-value exports including AI-related technology. Despite improving loss ratios, the market remained soft. • Ocean hull premiums increased 9.4 percent to USD 10.5 billion, encouraged by global fleet growth, higher vessel values and war premiums. Fleet growth continued to outpace premium growth indicating continued competitive pressure although loss ratios appear to have normalised. • Offshore energy premiums were broadly unchanged at USD 4.82 billion, up just 0.1 percent on 2024. London retained a 62.7 percent market share of which around 30% is renewables. While the market remains soft, energy security and geopolitical concerns could support significant future investment. As in previous years, the report also provides an update on IUMI’s Major Claims Database which contains data from 2013 onward with 30 national insurance associations now contributing. The number of observations for cargo claims has grown to 7,200 and a cumulative loss of USD 11.4 billion. IUMI’s revised Hull Inflation Index, which helps insurers to explain marine repair cost inflation using a range of macroeconomic indicators, is also showcased. Commenting on this year’s report, IUMI Secretary General, Lars Lange said: “The 2025 marine insurance market recorded modest growth in global premiums, although underlying conditions remained soft. Increased capacity, competitive pressures and currency movements, particularly the weakness of the US dollar, all influenced reported premium levels. On the claims side, the overall picture remained relatively stable with no single catastrophic loss significantly affecting any individual sector. However, attritional claims continued to accumulate putting pressure on profitability. Concerns that global tariffs would significantly constrain international trade proved less pronounced than anticipated while global GDP growth was stronger than expected. At the same time, the global race for AI began to influence marine trade with high-value semiconductors becoming an increasingly important component of international cargo movements. Asia continued to lead market growth with premium income rising steadily since 2016 and China remaining the region’s dominant market. European markets also expanded, although at a slower pace. Looking ahead, geopolitical tensions continued to shape the market into 2026. War cover became increasingly prominent while vessel availability, particularly for energy carriers, tightened as conflict in the Middle East intensified. Strong oil and gas demand continued to support activity while the impact of global tariffs remained less significant than initially feared. At IUMI, our job is to keep abreast of these many issues and engage with the relevant agencies to ensure marine underwriters are aware and equipped to continue to provide the insurance and risk mitigation services that ensure global trade continues without interruption. Our annual Stats Report is compiled by our Facts & Figures Committee together with input from a number of valued data partners. My thanks go to them all.” The full report is available to download from the statistics section of the IUMI website: https://iumi.com/statistics/iumi-stats-report-2026/ Source: IUMI Tops 2026-10-28 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Tanker owners can’t call a $140m ship too old to upgrade, says BAR Technologies
articles.summary: With new VLCCs ordered today won’t be delivering until 2029, most of the ships that will carry the world’s oil this decade are already trading. Portsmouth, UK, 20 October 2026. With a 15-year-old tanker now worth more than a new one, owners have demolished their own favourite argument against retrofitting older...
articles.body: Tanker owners can’t call a $140m ship too old to upgrade, says BAR Technologies in International Shipping News 28/10/2026 With new VLCCs ordered today won’t be delivering until 2029, most of the ships that will carry the world’s oil this decade are already trading. Portsmouth, UK, 20 October 2026. With a 15-year-old tanker now worth more than a new one, owners have demolished their own favourite argument against retrofitting older ships, according to BAR Technologies CEO John Cooper. Poten & Partners values a VLCC available for prompt delivery at around $235 million, compared with approximately $130 million for a newbuilding ordered today and due for delivery in 2029. Even a 15-year-old VLCC could command around $140 million, according to the shipbroker. “The argument against retrofitting older ships has always been that it’s not worth spending money on a vessel near the end of its life,” said Cooper. “Well, the market has just put a $140 million price on a 15-year-old tanker. You can’t value a ship like that and then tell me it’s not worth improving.” Cooper expects many of those ships, some of which would have been heading for recycling within a few years, to keep trading into the 2030s. Every extra year is another year of fuel bills, and on a deep-sea ship, wind is, he says, “the only propulsion energy that’s free at source”. There is a regulatory argument, too. WindWings can reduce fuel consumption and CO₂ emissions, potentially improving a vessel’s Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) rating and helping owners maintain its commercial viability as efficiency requirements tighten. For owners extending the working lives of older ships rather than replacing them, wind propulsion offers a way to improve operational performance while reducing fuel costs, strengthening the case for life extension, not just fuel savings. John Cooper, CEO of BAR Technologies BAR has modelled what that means for a VLCC on a typical USA to JPN trade. A typical 5x 37.5m WindWings® installation would save around 2670 tonnes of fuel a year (at a utilisation rate of 80%), worth $2.27m ($850/t assuming VLSFO usage) in saved fuel costs, paying back in 4 years based on fuel savings alone (without accounting for any carbon-related costs or benefits). [If confirmed: The work can be done during a routine dry-docking.] The technology is already working on existing ships. The bulk carriers Pyxis Ocean and Berge Olympus were both retrofitted with WindWings, and DNV independently recorded up to a 32% cut in main engine energy use on Pyxis Ocean in favourable conditions. Union Maritime has taken delivery of three WindWings-equipped LR2 tankers, with two more due in 2027. “Shipping has spent ten years telling itself that decarbonisation happens on the order book,” said Cooper. “The order book is full until 2029. The ships that have to burn less fuel this decade are the ones sailing now. “So if the market is comfortable putting $140 million on a 15-year-old tanker, owners should be asking themselves whether it still makes sense not to spend a fraction of that improving the way it runs.” Source: BAR Technologies 2026-10-28 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: European Shipowners reiterate key asks for EU ETS negotiations in Council and Parliament
articles.summary: European shipping is a geopolitical asset for Europe, facilitating the export and import of goods, food and energy. articles.body: European Shipowners reiterate key asks for EU ETS negotiations in Council and Parliament in International Shipping News 28/10/2026 European shipping is a geopolitical asset for Europe, facilitating the export and import of goods, food and energy. While the EU represents around 15% of global GDP, the European fleet represents 34.5% of the world’s fleet in terms of global tonnage across all segments. As the European Parliament and the Council advance their work on the Commission proposal for the EU ETS revision, European Shipowners | ECSA highlight the key amendments needed for the revision to deliver on shipping’s energy transition while safeguarding the competitiveness of European shipping. A recent study found that shipping accounts for around 10% of EU ETS emissions but contributes almost 20% of ETS revenues. The new mechanism is an opportunity to reinvest part of this contribution in shipping’s energy transition. However, the 110 million allowances proposed by the Commission cover only a third of what is needed. We call on the policymakers to: • Reinvest ETS revenues in shipping’s decarbonisation. Shipping generates EUR 9 billion a year in national and EU ETS revenues. A recent study found that SMAP should be tripled from 110 million to 330 million allowances to help build a market for sustainable fuels and technologies. • Support all technologies. SMAP’s scope should be extended and cover all technologies that deliver carbon savings, including energy efficiency projects. • Make SMAP predictable. Predictability is essential: companies need certainty, before they take investment decisions, that the price gap between sustainable and conventional fuels and technologies will be partly covered. Companies should be able to apply for support for fuels and technologies in advance. • Reward EU production. SMAP should incentivise the production of fuels and technologies in Europe through bonus points rather than made-in-Europe requirements. • Earmark a dedicated envelope for shipping. The general earmarking of Member States’ ETS revenues should include a specific percentage or envelope for shipping. • Apply one system to offshore vessels. The Commission has rightly recognised the need to change the rules applicable to offshore vessels, including the port call definition, to address unfair competition from non-EU offshore companies. However, applying one system from 2027 to 2030 and a different one from 2031 creates an unnecessary administrative burden. Only the new rules should apply. • Maintain, extend and improve derogations. Derogations for islands, outermost regions, ice-class vessels and transnational public services/obligations must be maintained, extended and made fit for purpose to support local economies, connectivity and regional cohesion. • Support port competitiveness without distorting competition. ES|ECSA shares the objective of keeping EU ports competitive. To maintain a level playing field across all shipping segments, the transhipment exemption should be replaced by an annual Commission report on port competitiveness and infrastructure needs. Where needed, national ETS revenues should support port infrastructure upgrades. • Simplify the EU MRV Regulation. Simplifying the EU Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (MRV) Regulation is key to aligning the EU ETS, MRV and FuelEU Maritime, and to limiting the administrative burden on companies. “Shipping pays almost 20% of total ETS revenues, although it accounts for only 10% of the emissions covered by the system, and, unlike other sectors, it has never received a single free allowance. The European Parliament and the Council should at least triple the ETS revenues earmarked for SMAP to send a credible market signal for the scale-up of sustainable maritime fuels and technologies, including energy efficiency. Predictability is essential: companies need certainty, before they take investment decisions, that the price gap between sustainable and conventional fuels will be partly covered. We strongly welcome the new provisions for offshore vessels. However, there is no justification for maintaining two consecutive and completely different reporting and compliance systems for these vessels. This significantly increases the administrative burden and undermines the competitiveness of the European offshore sector”, said Sotiris Raptis, Secretary General of European Shipowners | ECSA. Source: European Shipowners | ECSA 2026-10-28 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

A recent study found that shipping accounts for around 10% of EU ETS emissions but contributes almost 20% of ETS revenues.
The new mechanism is an opportunity to reinvest part of this contribution in shipping’s energy transition.

articles.body: ENGINE: East of Suez Bunker Fuel Availability Outlook in International Shipping News 28/10/2026 Singapore and Malaysia Bunker fuel availability remains tight in Singapore, with constrained fuel oil inventories. Reduced supply flows and tightening inventories across East of Suez continue to weigh on availability at the port. VLSFO lead times start at around 13 days at the earliest, and some suppliers recommend more than three weeks. Lead times were 12-15 days last week. HSFO lead times stand at around 10 days but stretch to as long as three weeks, almost unchanged from last week. LSMGO needs 9-11 days, compared with 7-14 days last week. Bunker supply in Port Klang, Malaysia, stays constrained across multiple grades. Prompt VLSFO availability is particularly tight, LSMGO supply is limited and HSFO availability faces continued pressure. East Asia VLSFO and HSFO availability remains tight in Zhoushan despite subdued demand, with several suppliers reporting low inventories and reduced imports, a source said. VLSFO lead times have shortened to eight days from 12 days last week, while HSFO lead times remain unchanged at 12 days. LSMGO availability has improved, with lead times falling to around four days from 12 days a week earlier. Bunker operations across Zhoushan have been suspended since last week due to rough weather brought by Typhoon Champi, the source said. The more sheltered Xiushandong briefly resumed operations yesterday before suspending them again. Operations could resume on 28 October as weather conditions are expected to improve. Supply conditions vary across other Chinese ports. Dalian and Qingdao have sufficient VLSFO and LSMGO stocks, although HSFO availability remains tight in Qingdao. Tianjin is facing shortages across all three major fuel grades, while VLSFO and HSFO supplies are limited in Shanghai. LSMGO availability in Shanghai remains relatively stable. Supply constraints also persist in southern China, with suppliers in Fuzhou, Xiamen, Yangpu and Guangzhou reporting shortages of VLSFO and LSMGO. Hong Kong’s bunker market remains stable, with suppliers recommending lead times of around seven days for the major fuel grades. In Taiwan, VLSFO and LSMGO deliveries are available within two days at Keelung. Lead times are slightly longer at Hualien, Kaohsiung and Taichung, at around three days, largely unchanged from the previous week. Bunker demand has softened across South Korea as rising Brent futures have pushed benchmark prices higher. Busan’s VLSFO price has climbed by around $100/mt since the beginning of October to approximately $1,069/mt, according to a South Korean trader. At southern ports, including Busan, Ulsan, Masan, Onsan, Yeosu and Kwangyang, lead times for all major fuel grades have increased to around 5–8 days from 3–6 days a week earlier. In contrast, availability has improved at western ports, including Incheon, Daesan, Dangjin, Pyeongtaek and Taean. Lead times for VLSFO, LSMGO and HSFO at these ports have fallen to 5–8 days from around 15 days previously. Adverse weather could disrupt bunker operations at several South Korean ports in the coming days. Busan and Ulsan may face interruptions on 28 October, 30–31 October and 1–4 November. Operations at Yeosu could be affected from 30 October to 1 November, while Daesan may experience disruptions between 27 October-1 November. VLSFO and HSFO availability remains severely constrained at several Japanese ports, including Tokyo, Chiba, Kawasaki, Nagoya, Yokkaichi, Osaka, Kobe, Mizushima, Tokuyama and Oita, where VLSFO stocks are nearly depleted. Most offers are subject to enquiry, and VLSFO is available only through spot offers in Tokyo, Chiba and Kawasaki. Term slots have been cancelled at these ports. Kashima is also experiencing tight availability of VLSFO and HSFO. Oceania Bunker fuel supply remains stable in Western Australia, with VLSFO readily available at Kwinana and Fremantle. Suppliers at both ports recommend lead times of around seven days. Each port has only one supplier, and all bunker deliveries are made by barge. Supply conditions are mixed along Australia’s east coast. Port Kembla has normal VLSFO availability, with deliveries possible by truck or pipeline. Sydney has sufficient VLSFO and LSMGO stocks, although HSFO availability is tighter, with suppliers generally requiring around seven days’ notice. Brisbane and Gladstone have ample supplies of VLSFO and LSMGO, with lead times of approximately one week. In contrast, VLSFO availability has tightened in Melbourne and Geelong, where one supplier has reported that stocks are nearly depleted. The supplier is awaiting replenishment cargoes, with constraints expected to persist until the first week of November. HSFO availability has also tightened further in Melbourne and Brisbane. The approaching cyclone season could pose additional risks to bunker operations across Australia, a source said. Running from November to April, the season could disrupt fuel availability at ports nationwide. New Zealand’s bunker market remains broadly stable, with VLSFO readily available at Tauranga and Auckland. Suppliers at both ports are recommending lead times of around four days. At Marsden Point, vessels can receive VLSFO and LSMGO directly through the pipeline. Adverse weather remains the main operational risk in New Zealand, particularly in Wellington and ports across the South Island, where disruptions to marine operations could delay bunker deliveries. In Papua New Guinea, bunker fuel availability remains tight across all major grades at the ports of Rabaul and Lae. South Asia Weather-related disruptions are expected at India’s Visakhapatnam port from 27–31 October, potentially delaying bunker operations. Very severe cyclonic storm Arnab was located about 140 km from Kakinada and 170 km from Visakhapatnam at noon on Tuesday, according to the India Meteorological Department (IMD). The storm is expected to cross the coast just south of Yanam by Wednesday forenoon, bringing winds of 125–135 kmph and gusts of up to 150 kmph. A storm surge of 1–2 metres could inundate low-lying areas near Kakinada and Yanam. The intensifying cyclone is moving towards the Andhra Pradesh coast, prompting storm warnings at several ports. Kakinada Port has been placed under the highest-level warning, while Visakhapatnam, Gangavaram, Machilipatnam and Nizampatnam ports have received high-level maritime storm warnings. In Sri Lanka, intermittent weather-related disruptions are forecast at Colombo from 27–29 October and at Trincomalee from 27–30 October, potentially delaying bunker deliveries at both ports. Middle East “The Middle Eastern bunker market continues to face supply and operational challenges amid regional security concerns and disruptions to vessel movements,” a Middle East-based source said. “In the UAE, Fujairah and Khor Fakkan continue to experience supply constraints, particularly for LSMGO, alongside significant price volatility,” the source added. VLSFO availability in Fujairah has improved despite ongoing disruptions to vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz amid US-Iran tensions, a regional source said. However, supplies of LSMGO and HSFO remain limited. In Saudi Arabia, bunker demand has eased slightly, while fuel availability and delivery schedules vary by port. Jeddah generally maintains stable LSMGO supplies, although deliveries remain subject to confirmation. Adverse weather could intermittently disrupt bunkering operations at Jeddah on 30 October and at Yanbu on 29–30 October. LSMGO supplies remain stable at key Omani ports, including Salalah, Muscat, Duqm and Sohar. One supplier is recommending lead times of 1–2 days for standard stems, largely unchanged from the previous week. In Qatar, Ras Laffan continues to face supply restrictions, while bunker fuel inventories at Egypt’s Port Suez are critically low. Across the region, LSMGO availability, prices and lead times remain uncertain at several ports. Early enquiries are recommended to secure supplies and confirm delivery schedules on a case-by-case basis. Adverse weather is also expected to disrupt bunkering operations at Port Said on 29–30 October. Djibouti, meanwhile, is facing limited availability across the major fuel grades. articles.title: New Report Exposes Critical Need For Trusted Digital Seafarer Credentials
articles.summary: A comprehensive new report entitled Securing Trust: The Transition to Digital Seafarer Credentials, published by maritime technology research firm Thetius in partnership with Maritime Passport, reveals that the global shipping industry’s reliance on paper certificates and disconnected digital copies poses significant...
articles.body: New Report Exposes Critical Need For Trusted Digital Seafarer Credentials in International Shipping News 28/10/2026 A comprehensive new report entitled Securing Trust: The Transition to Digital Seafarer Credentials, published by maritime technology research firm Thetius in partnership with Maritime Passport, reveals that the global shipping industry’s reliance on paper certificates and disconnected digital copies poses significant operational, security, and administrative risks. With an estimated 2.57 million seafarers serving on more than 85,000 merchant ships worldwide, maritime professionals are still routinely required to carry physical copies of certificates weighing up to four kilograms. The report emphasises that simply converting physical documents into unstructured electronic PDFs or disconnected digital portals cannot solve the industry’s verification challenge. Rather, there is a need for a globally trusted, interoperable trust framework that offers high levels of security but does not create more work for the various stakeholders – especially seafarers. Front cover of Thetius/Maritime Passport report Photo credit: Thetius “As an ex-seafarer myself, I have long been advocating for greater use of digital technologies in ways that benefit seafarers, and this report highlights the ways in which digital verification can and must evolve. But it’s vital that we do this correctly,” explains Martin White, Co-Founder of Maritime Passport. “Remarkable advances in digital identity, biometrics and secure credential technologies make a transition to digital verification possible, but they also raise important questions around legitimacy, governance, interoperability and adoption. Interoperability is essential, but it must strengthen these principles, never compromise them.” “In a digital age, trust both in technology but also in chosen partners, is non-negotiable,” explains Peter Phillips, Co-Founder of Maritime Passport. “Moving from paper to digital means protecting a seafarer’s identity, qualifications, and ultimately their livelihood, while safeguarding highly sensitive personal information. Digital credentials must reinforce issuing authority while giving employers, inspectors, and other key stakeholders confidence that every credential is valid, up to date, and held by the rightful individual.” Key findings of the Report Heavy administrative burden: Verifying credentials for a single seafarer can take between one and two hours for crewing recruitment teams. A recent industry survey cited in the report found that port call document preparation averages 191 minutes, with 64% of port calls still relying on paper or mixed paper/digital submissions. Operational delays and livelihood risks: Physical certificates and sea service records remain highly vulnerable to loss or damage. Replacing lost paper credentials requires contacting multiple issuing authorities, during which time a seafarer is unable to work, leading to crew change disruptions and vessel delays. Security and fraud vulnerabilities: With thousands of training institutions and national formats worldwide, visual inspection of certificates is increasingly unreliable. Forged or fraudulently altered certificates, as well as revoked or expired credentials remaining in circulation, continue to pose safety and regulatory compliance risks. Scanned copies and PDFs do not fix this: credentials need to be linked to verified digital identities that can be checked independently. Data protection and privacy risks: Scanned copies of passports and personal qualification records are frequently emailed and stored indefinitely on vessel computers and company servers, creating significant data privacy and GDPR compliance risks. Accelerating regulatory momentum: Recent amendments to the STCW Convention (effective January 2025) officially define “original form” to include electronic formats. Additionally, the IMO Strategy on Maritime Digitalisation approved at FAL 50 underlines an urgent industry shift toward standardised, interoperable digital data exchange. Other findings from the report include the need to preserve the authority of credential issuers rather than build a single global platform, the operational benefits of verified credentials for crew changes, inspections and crewing teams, and the importance of cyber resilience and offline verification. Recommendations for industry adoption: Establish Common Rules: International bodies and flag states must agree on baseline standards for digital credential validity, verification, data protection, and dispute handling. Design for a Phased Transition: System must support paper, digital copies, and native digital credentials simultaneously as maritime organisations transition at different speeds. Prioritise Interoperability: Buyers and regulators should mandate open standards and exit capabilities to prevent vendor lock-in and isolated digital silos. Support Developing Nations: Infrastructure solutions must accommodate smaller or lower-resource administrations to prevent a digital divide within the seafaring workforce. Source: Thetius and Maritime Passport 2026-10-28 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: With an estimated 2.57 million seafarers serving on more than 85,000 merchant ships worldwide, maritime professionals are still routinely required to carry physical copies of certificates weighing up to four kilograms.
The report emphasises that simply converting physical documents into unstructured electronic PDFs or disconnected digital portals cannot solve the industry’s verification challenge.
Rather, there is a need for a globally trusted, interoperable trust framework that offers high levels of security but does not create more work for the various stakeholders – especially seafarers.
